countries.name: Greece
countries.tagline: Four thousand years of wine on islands and mountains, now poured as some of the most electric whites and age-worthy reds of the Mediterranean.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (vineyard area includes table grapes and currants; 2025 output recovered from 1.4 mhl in both 2023 and 2024, still below Greece's historical 2 to 4 mhl range)

countries.overview:
Greece is where European wine culture learned to talk about itself. The Mycenaeans wrote the word for wine in Linear B, Homer gave the sea its colour from it, and the classical symposium turned a jug of watered wine into the setting for philosophy. Chian and Thasian wines travelled the Mediterranean in stamped amphorae, and the island of Thasos passed some of the first known laws regulating the wine trade. When modern wine lovers argue about origin, place and authenticity, they are continuing a conversation that started here.

Then came a long interruption. Byzantine Monemvasia shipped sweet Malmsey to all of Europe through Venetian hands, but four centuries of Ottoman rule taxed and hemmed in viticulture, and the young Greek state of the nineteenth century grew currants and bulk wine rather than fine bottles. Retsina, resinated white wine with roots in antiquity, became the national carafe. Phylloxera arrived late, in Macedonia from 1898, and ravaged the mainland while sparing the volcanic and limestone islands where vines still grow on their own roots.

The modern story begins in 1971 with the first appellation law and accelerates after Greece joined the European Community in 1981, when its appellations entered the EU register. A generation of producers trained in Bordeaux, Burgundy and Dijon came home in the 1980s and 1990s: Evangelos Gerovassiliou, Yiannis Boutaris, the Tsantalis family, Leon Karatsalos and Yiannis Paraskevopoulos of Gaia, George Skouras, Yiannis Tselepos. Some planted Cabernet and Chardonnay; the more lasting achievement was rediscovering what Greece already had. Gerovassiliou saved Malagousia from near extinction, the Zafeirakis family put Limniona on labels, and Santorini's growers turned Assyrtiko into the Mediterranean's answer to Chablis.

That native palette is the reason to care. Greece counts somewhere around 300 indigenous varieties, and the important ones are genuinely distinct: Assyrtiko holds bone-dry acidity in a hot island summer; Xinomavro, the 'acid-black' grape of Macedonia, gives pale, tannic reds that smell of tomato leaf, olive and dried roses and age like Nebbiolo; Agiorgitiko, from Nemea, is soft, plummy and generous; Moschofilero from the high Mantinia plateau is a pink-skinned aromatic white of rose petal and citrus. Add Malagousia, Roditis, Savatiano, Vidiano, Robola, Limnio, Liatiko, Mavrodaphne and the Muscats of Samos, Patras and Limnos and you have one of the richest ampelographic collections in Europe.

Geography explains the range. Greece is four-fifths mountains, and altitude rather than latitude sets the style: Amyndeon in the far north-west grows grapes at 600 to 750 metres beside four lakes and makes sparkling wine, while Santorini's vines crouch in wind-woven baskets on bare pumice at sea level. The Ionian and Aegean seas temper the heat, the meltemi wind dries the islands, and limestone, schist, volcanic ash and red clay change every few kilometres. Thirty-three Protected Designations of Origin (PDOs) cover the classic places, from Naoussa and Nemea to the four Malvasia appellations created in 2011 to revive the medieval sweet wine trade, and more than a hundred Protected Geographical Indications (PGIs) give room to blends and international grapes.

The recent news is climatic. The 2023 and 2024 harvests each fell to about 1.4 million hectolitres, among the smallest in modern records, after heatwaves, drought and wildfires; Santorini's 2024 crop was tiny even by its own miserly standards, and prices for island Assyrtiko have climbed accordingly. The OIV puts the 2025 harvest at 1.6 million hectolitres, a partial recovery that still leaves Greece well below its historical two to four million. The upside is a country that already farms some of the most heat-resilient grapes in Europe, and a wave of growers working old vines on their own roots, high-altitude sites and forgotten varieties. For a wine nerd, Greece is a place where the most ancient story and the newest bottle are often the same thing.

history.title: Pressed grapes at Dikili Tash
history.text: Charred grape pips and pressed skins in a Late Neolithic house at Dikili Tash, near Philippi in eastern Macedonia, are among the earliest evidence of grape pressing in the Aegean, more than a thousand years before the palaces of Crete.

history.title: Minoan presses and the buried town of Akrotiri
history.text: The Minoan villa at Vathypetro above Archanes kept a stone wine press and storage jars, and on Thera the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri was sealed with its jars and vessels under volcanic ash by the great eruption. The same pumice now feeds Santorini's ungrafted Assyrtiko.

history.title: Wine in Linear B
history.text: Mycenaean clay tablets from the Palace of Nestor at Pylos and from Knossos use an ideogram for wine and record vineyards, wine rations and a palace wine magazine with dozens of storage jars: the first written Greek wine administration.

history.title: Thasos regulates the wine trade
history.text: Inscriptions from Thasos set rules on when and how Thasian wine could be sold and shipped, and its stamped amphorae turn up across the Black Sea and the Aegean. It is one of the earliest legal frameworks for a named wine.

history.title: Chian wine, the classical grand cru
history.text: Wine from the Ariousian hills of Chios was the luxury bottle of the classical world, shipped in distinctive amphorae with a swollen neck and stamped with a sphinx. Athenian comedy and Roman writers treated it as the benchmark.

history.title: Malmsey sails from Monemvasia
history.text: From the fortified rock of Monemvasia, Venetian merchants shipped a sweet wine that Europe called Malvasia, Malvoisie or Malmsey. The name outlived the trade and attached itself to grapes from Madeira to the Lipari islands.

history.title: Gustav Clauss builds Achaia Clauss
history.text: A Bavarian merchant founded a castle-like winery in the hills above Patras and made a fortified red from Mavrodaphne that became Greece's best-known export wine of the nineteenth century.

history.title: Phylloxera reaches Macedonia
history.text: The louse arrived late, devastating the northern mainland vineyards in the early twentieth century, while Santorini's ash, Kefalonia's limestone scree and other islands stayed free of it, which is why ungrafted, centuries-old root systems survive there.

history.title: The first appellation law
history.text: Greece created its system of quality appellations, with Nemea and Naoussa among the first zones delimited. After accession to the European Community in 1981 the appellations entered the EU register.

history.title: Domaine Carras and the birth of modern Greek wine
history.text: John Carras planted a modern estate on the slopes of Mount Meliton in Sithonia with advice from Émile Peynaud; the Slopes of Meliton appellation followed in 1982. The estate also helped rescue Malagousia, which Evangelos Gerovassiliou, its winemaker, later made famous at Epanomi.

history.title: The Malvasia appellations return
history.text: Four PDOs were registered for sweet wines from sun-dried grapes in the medieval Malvasia tradition: Monemvasia-Malvasia, Malvasia Paros, Malvasia Sitia and Malvasia Chandakas-Candia.

history.title: Heat, drought and two tiny harvests
history.text: Greece produced about 1.4 million hectolitres in both 2023 and 2024, its smallest crops in modern records, before a partial recovery to 1.6 million in 2025 according to the OIV.

countries.classification:
Greek wine labels follow the EU pyramid. At the top sit the 33 PDOs (ΠΟΠ, Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis), most registered in 1981 when Greece joined the European Community; their rules fix varieties, yields and styles, and several are tied to a single grape (Naoussa to Xinomavro, Nemea to Agiorgitiko, Mantinia to Moschofilero, Patra to Roditis). Below them more than a hundred PGIs (ΠΓΕ) range from regional names such as Macedonia or Peloponnese to small zones such as Florina, Drama or Plagies Ampelou on Samos, and allow international varieties and blends. Varietal wines without geographical indication and plain wine sit at the bottom.

Three things trip up newcomers. First, many of the best bottles are PGIs, because estates blend native and international grapes or work outside a PDO's grape rules. Second, Greece keeps traditional terms: Retsina is protected as a 'traditional appellation' for resinated wine, Verdea for the oxidative whites of Zakynthos, and Vinsanto belongs to Santorini alone. Third, ageing words differ by category: Reserve and Grand Reserve are reserved for PDO wines, while Cava is used for aged PGI and table wines. Ktima means estate, Monastiri a monastery, Archontiko a manor.
countries.climate_soils:
A Mediterranean climate is bent out of shape by mountains and seas. Most vineyards sit between sea level and 1,000 metres, and altitude decides ripeness: Amyndeon (570 to 750 m) and Mantinia (around 650 m) are cool enough for sparkling wine, while the Peloponnese coast and Crete are hot and dry. The northern meltemi blows across the Aegean all summer, cooling the islands and keeping disease pressure low, but it also forces growers into low bush vines and, on Santorini, into woven baskets.

Soils are a mosaic. Santorini has volcanic ash and pumice with almost no clay, which is why phylloxera never took hold; Kefalonia's Robola grows in limestone scree on Mount Ainos; Naoussa mixes marl, clay and limestone with sandy patches; Nemea runs from red clay on the valley floor to limestone and stony soils at 600 to 850 metres; Crete offers calcareous marls and clay. Water stress is the defining modern problem, and drought farming of old, low-yielding bush vines is both a tradition and a climate strategy.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.note: Santorini's flagship white, now planted all over Greece and abroad; holds piercing acidity and saline, smoky intensity even in heat. The basis of dry Santorini, Nykteri and Vinsanto.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.note: The great red of Macedonia (Naoussa, Amyndeon, Goumenissa, Rapsani): pale, tannic and acidic, with tomato, olive and dried-rose aromas; long-lived and often compared with Nebbiolo.

grapes.name: Agiorgitiko
grapes.note: Nemea's red: soft tannins, plum and cherry fruit, versatile from rosé to oak-aged reserves and sweet styles.

grapes.name: Moschofilero
grapes.note: Pink-skinned aromatic white from the Mantinia plateau: rose, citrus and spice with crisp acidity; also made as sparkling and rosé.

grapes.name: Malagousia
grapes.note: Aromatic white rescued from near extinction in the 1970s and popularised by Gerovassiliou at Epanomi: peach, jasmine and herbs.

grapes.name: Roditis
grapes.note: Pink-skinned white, widely planted, the sole grape of PDO Patra and a component of Anchialos and much retsina.

grapes.name: Savatiano
grapes.note: Greece's most planted white, the backbone of Attica and of retsina; old dry-farmed vines give surprisingly textured, lemony wines.

grapes.name: Limniona
grapes.note: Ancient Thessalian red revived by the Zafeirakis family at Tyrnavos: fresh, peppery and silky.

grapes.name: Mavrodaphne
grapes.note: Dark red of Patras and Kefalonia, famous for fortified sweet wines, increasingly made dry.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
grapes.note: Moschato Aspro: the grape of Muscat of Samos, Patras, Rio Patras, Kefalonia and Rhodes.

grapes.name: Muscat of Alexandria
grapes.note: Moschato Alexandreias: the grape of Limnos, made dry and sweet.

grapes.name: Robola
grapes.note: Limestone-loving white of Kefalonia, lemony and stony.

grapes.name: Vidiano and Vilana
grapes.note: Crete's whites: Vidiano is the rising star (apricot, herbs, texture), Vilana the traditional base of Peza.

grapes.name: Liatiko, Kotsifali and Mandilaria
grapes.note: Crete's reds: Liatiko (pale, spicy, often sweet) in Dafnes and Sitia; Kotsifali softened by deep-coloured Mandilaria in Peza and Archanes.

grapes.name: Limnio
grapes.note: Probably the Lemnia vine of Aristotle; grown on Limnos and in Halkidiki (Slopes of Meliton).

grapes.name: Debina
grapes.note: High-acid white of Zitsa in Epirus, made still and lightly sparkling.

countries.name: Cyprus
countries.tagline: The island of Commandaria, the oldest named wine still made, and of phylloxera-free mountain vines.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figures: 6,040 ha of vines in 2024 and 10,800 t of wine (about 0.11 mhl) in 2022. Not reported separately in the OIV 2025 report

countries.overview:
Cyprus has made wine for at least five thousand years and has kept one wine name for more than eight hundred. Residues in Chalcolithic flasks from Erimi, near Limassol, analysed in 2005, point to wine around 3500 BC, and the Bronze Age site of Pyrgos-Mavroraki had a winery beside its perfume workshop. Hesiod described drying grapes in the sun before making sweet wine, the method still used in the island's great dessert wine, Commandaria.

Commandaria takes its name from the Grande Commanderie, the estate around Kolossi castle held by the Knights Templar and then the Knights Hospitaller from the late twelfth century. The knights shipped the sweet amber wine to Europe's courts and to pilgrims bound for the Holy Land, which is why Commandaria claims to be the oldest named wine still in production. Legend adds that Richard the Lionheart called it 'the wine of kings and the king of wines' at his wedding in Limassol in 1191, and that a sweet Cypriot wine, widely believed to be Commandaria, won 'La Bataille des Vins', the tasting staged by the French king and recorded in Henri d'Andeli's poem of about 1224. In December 2025 UNESCO inscribed Commandaria's traditions in the 14 villages on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The modern industry was built on volume. British rule after 1878, the island's freedom from phylloxera (strict quarantine kept the louse out) and cheap fortified 'Cyprus sherry' made Cyprus one of Britain's leading wine suppliers by the 1960s, while big Limassol companies (KEO, ETKO, LOEL, SODAP) shipped bulk wine to the Soviet bloc. When those markets collapsed in the 1980s and 1990s, the state paid for small regional wineries in the Troodos villages, and the island began bottling its own grapes: the red Maratheftiko and Yiannoudi, the white Xynisteri and Promara, alongside the workhorse Mavro.

Today about 50 to 60 wineries work mostly on the southern slopes of the Troodos mountains, between 600 and 1,500 metres, where vines grow on their own roots in limestone, chalk and volcanic soils. The island has seven PDOs: Commandaria plus six regional zones (Pitsilia, Vouni Panagias-Ambelitis, Laona Akama and the three Krasochoria Lemesou zones). The island's division since 1974 means all of the PDOs lie in the south; the north has a few vineyards but no EU-registered appellations.

history.title: Wine in Erimi's flasks
history.text: Chalcolithic round-bottomed flasks excavated at Erimi in the 1930s were analysed in 2005 and showed traces consistent with wine, among the earliest in the Mediterranean. The Cyprus Wine Museum stands in the village.

history.title: Pyrgos-Mavroraki winery
history.text: Excavations at Pyrgos-Mavroraki in the Limassol hills found a Bronze Age industrial complex with a perfumery, an olive press and a winery with grape seeds and storage vessels.

history.title: Hesiod's sun-dried grapes
history.text: Hesiod's Works and Days describes laying grapes in the sun for ten days before pressing, the technique still used for Commandaria.

history.title: Richard the Lionheart in Limassol
history.text: Richard I married Berengaria of Navarre in Limassol; tradition says he praised the island's sweet wine as 'the wine of kings and the king of wines'. He then sold Cyprus to the Templars.

history.title: The Battle of the Wines
history.text: Henri d'Andeli's poem La Bataille des Vins records a tasting held for the French king; the winner was a sweet wine of Cyprus, traditionally identified as Commandaria.

history.title: The Grande Commanderie at Kolossi
history.text: The Knights Hospitaller ran their main Cypriot estate from Kolossi castle (the present keep dates from 1454) and shipped its sweet wine to Europe, giving Commandaria its name.

history.title: Phylloxera-free boom and Cyprus sherry
history.text: Under British rule and with European vineyards destroyed by phylloxera, Cyprus exported grapes and wine; 'Cyprus sherry', first sold under that name in 1937, made the island Britain's third-biggest wine supplier by the 1960s.

history.title: Commandaria's appellation law
history.text: A law of 2 March 1990 limited Commandaria to 14 villages on the southern slopes of the Troodos; the EU registered it as a PDO.

history.title: UNESCO recognises Commandaria
history.text: In December 2025 UNESCO inscribed Commandaria wine and its traditions on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, Cyprus's seventh element on the list.

countries.classification: Cyprus follows the EU system: seven PDOs (ΠΟΠ, OEOP on older labels) and four regional PGIs named after the districts (Lemesos, Pafos, Larnaka, Lefkosia). Commandaria's rules are among the strictest in Europe: only Xynisteri and Mavro from 14 named villages, goblet-trained and unirrigated vines at least four years old, harvest only when the Vine Products Commission gives the signal, grapes sun-dried (usually 7 to 10 days) to 390 to 450 grams of sugar per litre, and at least two years in oak. The six regional PDOs require vineyards above about 600 to 750 metres, low yields and minimum vine ages.
countries.climate_soils: A hot, dry Mediterranean island climate is cooled by altitude: the Troodos range rises to 1,952 metres at Mount Olympus, and almost all quality vineyards sit on its southern and western slopes between 400 and 1,500 metres. Soils are chalk and limestone (Laona, the Krasochoria), with igneous and volcanic soils on the higher Troodos (Pitsilia). Phylloxera has never reached Cyprus, so vines grow ungrafted.

grapes.name: Mavro
grapes.note: The most planted red, high-yielding and rustic, but the essential partner in Commandaria.

grapes.name: Xynisteri
grapes.note: The main white: fresh, citrus and saline at altitude; the other Commandaria grape.

grapes.name: Maratheftiko
grapes.note: Deep-coloured, structured native red, the island's flagship for quality reds (needs a pollinator: the flowers are functionally female).

grapes.name: Yiannoudi
grapes.note: Rare native red rediscovered in the 2000s, fresh and spicy.

grapes.name: Promara
grapes.note: Rescued native white, aromatic and fresh.

grapes.name: Spourtiko and Morokanella
grapes.note: Rare native whites, part of the revival.

grapes.name: Ofthalmo
grapes.note: Light native red.

countries.name: Malta
countries.tagline: Tiny limestone islands with two native grapes, Ġellewża and Girgentina, and two island appellations.

stats.note: NSO Malta via FAOSTAT (official figure): 420 ha of vines in 2024. Production is small and not reported by OIV (about 630 tonnes of wine in 2005 per Wikipedia)

countries.overview:
Malta's wine history is Phoenician, Roman and then, for a long time, imported. The modern industry dates from the early twentieth century, when Emmanuel Delicata (1907) and Marsovin (1919) were founded near Paola, but for decades they relied on imported grapes and must. Accession to the EU in 2004 removed protective levies and pushed the islands towards quality: international varieties were planted from the 1970s and especially the 1990s, and estates such as Meridiana (1987), Montekristo, Ta' Betta and Ta' Mena on Gozo now bottle wines from local vineyards.

The point of interest is the two native grapes. Ġellewża is a light, red-fruited black grape often made as rosé or frizzante; Girgentina is a delicate, low-alcohol white. Both are found almost nowhere else. Malta and Gozo each have a PDO (DOK, Denominazzjoni ta' Oriġini Kontrollata), and the Maltese Islands IĠT covers the whole archipelago. Vineyards are small, terraced and walled against the wind, on thin soils over globigerina and coralline limestone, and the hot, dry, windy summers make irrigation and early harvests common.

history.title: Phoenician vines
history.text: Phoenician traders settled Malta and are thought to have introduced the vine; Roman villas such as the one at Rabat later had wine presses.

history.title: Delicata and Marsovin
history.text: Emmanuel Delicata (1907) and Marsovin (1919), both based near Paola, founded Malta's commercial wine industry.

history.title: EU membership and the DOK system
history.text: After accession in 2004 Malta adopted EU wine rules; the PDOs Malta and Gozo were registered in 2009.

countries.classification: Two PDOs (DOK Malta and DOK Gozo/Għawdex) and one PGI (IĠT Maltese Islands). DOK wines must come from registered local vineyards with lower yields than IĠT.
countries.climate_soils: Hot, dry summers, mild winters, strong winds; thin terra rossa and carbonate soils over globigerina and coralline limestone.

grapes.name: Ġellewża
grapes.note: Native red, light and fruity, often made as rosé or sparkling.

grapes.name: Girgentina
grapes.note: Native white, delicate and low in alcohol, sometimes blended with Chardonnay.

grapes.name: Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Vermentino
grapes.note: Main international varieties.

countries.name: Türkiye
countries.tagline: The world's sixth-largest vineyard, almost all for eating, with a small and stubborn wine scene built on Öküzgözü, Boğazkere, Kalecik Karası and Emir.

stats.note: OIV 2025: 395 kha of vines, the sixth largest vineyard in the world, but mostly table grapes and raisins (Sultaniye); only a small share of the crop, estimated at 3 to 15 percent, is made into wine. Wine output below the OIV's 1 mhl reporting threshold.

countries.overview:
Anatolia is one of the places where the grapevine was domesticated, and wine runs through its ancient history: Hittite laws of the second millennium BC fined anyone who damaged a vineyard, Assyrian merchants at Kültepe traded wine, the Phrygians and Lydians shipped it across the Aegean, and the Ionian coast was Dionysus's home ground. Under the Ottomans, commercial winemaking was the business of non-Muslim communities (Greeks, Armenians, Syriacs and Jews), and the population exchanges and expulsions of the early twentieth century took much of that knowledge with them.

The Republic restarted the industry from the top. Atatürk ordered a state winery at Tekirdağ in 1925, the Tekel monopoly controlled alcohol for most of the century, and the private houses that still dominate, Doluca (1926) and Kavaklıdere (1929), date from those years. Tekel's wine division was privatised in 2004 (its successor, Kayra, owns the historic Buzbağ brand), and a wave of new estates in Thrace, on the Aegean and in Cappadocia began replanting native grapes alongside Cabernet and Merlot. There are now roughly 140 licensed wineries.

The native grapes are the reason to pay attention. Öküzgözü ('ox eye') from Elazığ is juicy and bright; Boğazkere ('throat-scratcher') from Diyarbakır is dark and tannic, and the two together are the classic Turkish red blend. Kalecik Karası, rescued by Ankara University in the 1960s and 1970s from near extinction, makes pale, perfumed, Pinot-like reds near Ankara. Emir grows on the volcanic tuff of Cappadocia and gives crisp, mineral whites and traditional-method sparkling; Narince, from Tokat, gives fuller whites. On the Aegean, Urla Karası and Bornova Misketi have been brought back from near extinction.

The obstacle is policy. Since a 2013 law, alcohol advertising and promotion are banned, producers cannot advertise or even show their wines in most media, sales are restricted at night and near schools and mosques, and special consumption tax is among the highest in Europe and is revised upward regularly. Domestic consumption is tiny (about one litre per person a year), so the industry lives from tourism, the urban middle class and a small export trade.

history.title: Wine in the Assyrian colony at Kültepe
history.text: Clay tablets from the Old Assyrian merchant colony at Kültepe (Kanesh), near Kayseri, record wine among the goods traded across Anatolia.

history.title: Hittite vineyard laws
history.text: Hittite law codes from Hattusa set penalties for damaging vineyards and ritual texts describe wine libations to the gods.

history.title: Atatürk's state winery
history.text: The new Republic ordered a state winery at Tekirdağ in Thrace; Tekel later held the alcohol monopoly.

history.title: Doluca and Kavaklıdere
history.text: The two private houses that still lead the industry were founded in Thrace (Doluca at Mürefte) and Ankara (Kavaklıdere).

history.title: Tekel's wine business privatised
history.text: The state monopoly's alcoholic drinks division was privatised; its wineries became Kayra, and a generation of boutique estates followed.

history.title: The alcohol advertising ban
history.text: Law 6487 banned alcohol advertising and promotion and restricted retail sales between 22:00 and 06:00, sharply limiting how Turkish wineries can reach customers.

countries.classification: Türkiye has no operational appellation system for wine comparable to the EU's; labels name grapes, wineries and broad regions (Thrace, Aegean, Cappadocia, Eastern Anatolia). A few geographical indications exist for grapes and other products, and producer groups such as Thrace's 'Trakya' wine route promote regional identity.
countries.climate_soils: Four broad zones: maritime Thrace and the Marmara coast; the Mediterranean Aegean coast and its hotter inland plateaus (Denizli, Manisa); continental Central Anatolia at 800 to 1,200 metres, including Cappadocia's volcanic tuff, where growers sometimes bury vines against winter frost; and the hot, dry, high Euphrates valley of Eastern Anatolia (Elazığ, Malatya, Diyarbakır).

grapes.name: Öküzgözü
grapes.note: Elazığ's 'ox-eye' red: juicy, bright, low tannin.

grapes.name: Boğazkere
grapes.note: Diyarbakır's tannic, dark red; blended with Öküzgözü in Buzbağ and many modern reds.

grapes.name: Kalecik Karası
grapes.note: Pale, perfumed red from the Kızılırmak valley near Ankara, revived from near extinction.

grapes.name: Emir
grapes.note: Cappadocia's crisp white, still and sparkling.

grapes.name: Narince
grapes.note: Fuller white from Tokat, also used for stuffed vine leaves.

grapes.name: Papazkarası and Yapıncak
grapes.note: Thrace's native red and white.

grapes.name: Urla Karası and Bornova Misketi
grapes.note: Aegean grapes revived around İzmir.

grapes.name: Sultaniye
grapes.note: The seedless raisin grape of Manisa and Denizli, mostly for drying.

countries.name: Lebanon
countries.tagline: Phoenician wine, Roman temples and Jesuit cellars, made every vintage through war in the high Bekaa.

stats.note: Wine-grape area approximate (roughly 2,000 to 3,000 ha of wine grapes; total vineyard including table grapes is larger). Lebanese wineries produced about 15 million bottles in 2024 despite the war, per press reports cited on Wikipedia; the Union Vinicole du Liban has estimated around 9 million bottles in normal years.

countries.overview:
Lebanon is the coast that taught the Mediterranean to trade wine. Phoenician ports at Byblos, Tyre and Sidon shipped wine to Old Kingdom Egypt, and Phoenician sailors carried vines and amphorae to Carthage, Sicily, Sardinia and Spain; a seventh-century BC wine press at Tell el-Burak near Sidon shows production for export. The prophet Hosea compared Israel's future fame to 'the wine of Lebanon'. Under Rome, the great sanctuary at Baalbek in the Bekaa included the Temple of Bacchus, one of the best-preserved Roman temples anywhere, its doorway carved with vines and grapes.

Four centuries of Ottoman rule kept commercial wine to Christian communities making it for the church. The modern revival began in the Bekaa in the mid-nineteenth century: Château Ksara was founded by Jesuits in 1857 near Zahlé, and in 1898 they found the Roman-era caves that are now its cellar; Domaine des Tourelles followed in 1868. The French Mandate created a market for wine in Beirut, and in 1930 Gaston Hochar founded Château Musar at Ghazir, north of Beirut. His son Serge, Bordeaux-trained under Émile Peynaud, made Musar from 1959 until his death in 2014 and turned it into one of the cult wines of the world after Michael Broadbent picked the 1967 at the Bristol Wine Fair of 1979.

The legend of Lebanese wine is resilience. Through the civil war of 1975 to 1990, Musar missed only one vintage (1976); in 1982 its Bekaa vineyards lay on the front line between Syrian and Israeli tanks; in 2006 and again in 2024 harvests went on under airstrikes. Since the 1990s the number of wineries has grown from a handful to around 50 to 60, with Kefraya, Massaya, Ixsir, Domaine Wardy, Château Marsyas, Atibaia and many small producers. Most vineyards are in the Bekaa at about 900 to 1,200 metres, between the Mount Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, with newer high vineyards in Batroun, Jezzine and Mount Lebanon.

Two native white grapes, Obaideh and Merwah, give Lebanon its own voice (they are the white in Château Musar Blanc), and producers are reviving others such as Zeini, Meksassi, Asmi Noir and Sabbagieh. Reds are mostly Cinsault, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre, with a warm, spicy character from sun and altitude.

history.title: Byblos wine for the pharaohs
history.text: Wine from Byblos and the Phoenician coast was shipped to Old Kingdom Egypt, one of the earliest long-distance wine trades.

history.title: The wine press of Tell el-Burak
history.text: Excavations near Sidon found a large plastered Phoenician wine press with vineyards nearby, built to produce wine for overseas trade.

history.title: The Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek
history.text: Rome built the Temple of Bacchus within the sanctuary of Heliopolis in the Bekaa, its stone carved with vines, grapes and drinking scenes.

history.title: Jesuits found Château Ksara
history.text: Jesuit priests planted vines at Ksara near Zahlé; in 1898 they found Roman-era caves, now two kilometres of cellars.

history.title: Gaston Hochar founds Château Musar
history.text: Hochar, back from Bordeaux, set up Musar in an eighteenth-century castle at Ghazir; his son Serge took over winemaking in 1959.

history.title: Musar discovered at Bristol
history.text: Michael Broadbent named the 1967 Château Musar the discovery of the Bristol Wine Fair, opening the UK market.

history.title: Vintages through civil war
history.text: Lebanese wineries kept harvesting through the civil war; Musar missed only 1976.

history.title: Harvest under fire
history.text: Israeli strikes hit the Bekaa during the 2024 war; producers still harvested and bottled around 15 million bottles.

countries.classification: Lebanon has no appellation system. It joined the OIV in 1996, and the producers' association Union Vinicole du Liban, founded in 1997, promotes common standards and exports; labels carry winery names and broad regions (Bekaa Valley, Batroun, Mount Lebanon) rather than regulated appellations.

Soils are limestone, clay and gravel, red in places. Coastal and Mount Lebanon vineyards (Batroun, Jezzine, Kesrouan) climb to 1,400 metres and more, with more maritime influence.

countries.name: Israel
countries.tagline: Bronze Age palace cellars, Rothschild's colonies and a modern industry that took winemaking up the Golan and into the desert.

stats.note: Central Bureau of Statistics via FAOSTAT (official figure): 8,380 ha of grapes in 2024, table and wine; wine grapes are roughly 5,000 to 5,500 ha, with some 300 wineries producing around 40 million bottles. Not reported separately in OIV 2025

countries.overview:
Wine in the land of Israel is ancient, biblical and, after a long gap, very new. The Canaanite palace at Tel Kabri in western Galilee held a wine cellar of about 1700 BC with some 40 large jars and roughly 2,000 litres of wine flavoured with resins, honey and herbs: the oldest and largest palatial wine cellar known in the Near East. The Bible is full of vineyards and presses; Byzantine Gaza and Ashkelon exported wine across the Mediterranean, and in the Negev the Nabataean and Byzantine towns of Avdat and Shivta had large wine presses.

Islamic rule from the seventh century ended commercial wine for a millennium, though local grapes survived in Arab vineyards as table grapes and raisins. The modern industry was founded by Baron Edmond de Rothschild, owner of Château Lafite, who in the 1880s funded Jewish agricultural colonies and built wineries at Rishon LeZion (1890) and Zichron Ya'akov (1892), the origin of Carmel. For a century the industry made mostly sweet sacramental kosher wine.

The turn came in the late 1970s and 1980s, when University of California, Davis researchers identified the Golan Heights as a cool, high site, and the Golan Heights Winery (founded 1983, Yarden label) proved it with modern Cabernet, Chardonnay and sparkling wine. Domaine du Castel in the Judean Hills, Margalit, Yatir in the Negev, Clos de Gat, Recanati, Tzora and Flam followed, and the country now has about 300 wineries. The regions run from the Upper Galilee and the Golan (vineyards up to about 1,200 metres) through the Judean Hills and the Shomron to the Negev desert, where drip irrigation and high plateaus make viticulture possible.

Two features make Israel distinctive. Almost all large wineries are kosher, which involves rules on who handles the wine (Sabbath-observant Jews from crushing onward, unless the wine is heat-treated, mevushal), on fining agents and on agricultural laws such as orlah (no fruit from vines under four years) and shmita (the sabbatical year). And a research programme led by Ariel University and others has identified and revived ancient local grapes, among them Marawi (also called Hamdani), Jandali and Dabouki, as well as the red Bittuni, with Recanati and Cremisan bottling them.

Some of Israel's best-known vineyards lie in territory whose status is disputed. The Golan Heights were captured from Syria in 1967 and annexed by Israel in 1981, an annexation not recognised by the UN or most states (the United States recognised it in 2019); Israeli wineries in the West Bank are in territory considered occupied under international law. The EU requires that products from these areas not be labelled simply 'Made in Israel'.

history.title: The palace cellar at Tel Kabri
history.text: In 2013 excavators uncovered a storeroom in the Canaanite palace with about 40 large jars, around 2,000 litres in total, holding residues of a resinated, flavoured red wine.

history.title: Wine of Gaza and the Negev
history.text: Byzantine wine from Gaza and the Negev towns of Shivta and Avdat, which had large stone presses, was exported in 'Gaza jars' across the Mediterranean.

history.title: Mikveh Israel
history.text: The first Jewish agricultural school was founded near Jaffa and taught viticulture.

history.title: Rothschild's wineries
history.text: Baron Edmond de Rothschild funded the colonies of Rishon LeZion and Zichron Ya'akov and built their wineries (1890 and 1892), the core of Carmel.

history.title: The Golan Heights Winery
history.text: Founded at Katzrin after UC Davis advice identified the high Golan as a cool site; its Yarden wines started Israel's quality era.

history.title: Ancient grapes revived
history.text: DNA research identified local varieties such as Marawi (Hamdani), Jandali, Dabouki and Bittuni; Recanati bottled a Marawi from the 2014 vintage.

countries.classification: Israel has an official list of wine regions (Galil with the Golan, Upper and Lower Galilee subregions; Shomron; Shimshon; the Judean Hills; and the Negev) used on labels, but no appellation system with yield or grape rules. Kosher certification (and mevushal status) is the most visible label distinction.
countries.climate_soils: Mediterranean, with rainy winters and dry summers; every vineyard needs drip irrigation in summer. Quality depends on altitude: the Golan's basalt and volcanic tuff at 400 to 1,200 metres, Upper Galilee's limestone and terra rossa, the Judean Hills' limestone at 500 to 900 metres, and loess and sand in the Negev at up to 800 metres.

grapes.note: The main reds; old-vine Carignan and Petite Sirah are local specialities.

grapes.note: Main whites; Chardonnay for traditional-method sparkling on the Golan.

grapes.note: Ancient local whites revived from Arab vineyards.

grapes.name: Argaman
grapes.note: An Israeli cross (Carignan by Souzão) bred for colour.

countries.name: Palestine
countries.tagline: Monastic and family wineries in the West Bank keeping Hebron's ancient grapes alive.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official figure: 2,912 ha of grapes in 2021, mostly table grapes around Hebron; very small wine production from a handful of wineries

countries.overview:
The hills of Hebron and Bethlehem have grown grapes since antiquity, and Palestinian farmers kept local varieties alive as table grapes and raisins through centuries when wine was not made commercially. Today a few wineries operate in the West Bank. The Salesian monastery of Cremisan, on the edge of Beit Jala near Bethlehem, has made wine since 1885 and bottles single-variety wines from the ancient local grapes Hamdani, Jandali, Dabouki and Baladi, sourced from Palestinian growers around Hebron. In the Christian village of Taybeh, north-east of Ramallah, the Khoury family, known for Palestine's first craft brewery (1994), opened Taybeh Winery in 2013.

Winemaking here is shaped by occupation: checkpoints, permits and the separation barrier affect access to vineyards and markets. The Cremisan valley itself has been the subject of a long legal and political dispute over the barrier's route through monastery and village land.

history.text: Italian Salesian monks set up a winery at the Cremisan monastery near Beit Jala.

history.title: Ancient grapes bottled
history.text: With Italian oenologist Riccardo Cotarella's advice, Cremisan began releasing varietal Hamdani, Jandali, Dabouki and Baladi.

history.title: Taybeh Winery opens
history.text: The Khoury family added a winery to their Taybeh brewery in the Christian village north-east of Ramallah.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Mediterranean hill climate at 700 to 1,000 metres around Hebron and Bethlehem; limestone and terra rossa; dry farming of old bush vines is common.

grapes.name: Hamdani and Jandali
grapes.note: Ancient whites from the Hebron hills, often blended.

grapes.name: Dabouki
grapes.note: White grape thought to be among the oldest local varieties.

grapes.name: Baladi
grapes.note: Local red.

countries.name: Syria
countries.tagline: From the wine lists of Ugarit and Mari to Domaine de Bargylus, made through civil war in the Jebel Ansariyeh.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 43,713 ha of grapes in 2024, nearly all table grapes and raisins; wine production tiny, no reliable statistics

countries.overview:
Syria's wine history begins in the Bronze Age archives. Tablets from the palace of Mari on the Euphrates (eighteenth century BC) record wine shipments and the king's taste for good vintages; Ugarit on the coast traded wine across the eastern Mediterranean; and Ebla's archives mention vineyards. Under Rome and Byzantium, the north Syrian 'dead cities' of the limestone massif were wealthy olive and wine towns.

Modern Syrian wine is almost a single estate. Domaine de Bargylus, founded by the Lebanese Saadé brothers (also owners of Château Marsyas in the Bekaa) in 2003 on the slopes of the Jebel Ansariyeh near Latakia, at about 900 metres, makes Bordeaux- and Rhône-style blends; through the civil war from 2011 its owners managed the estate remotely and grapes were sometimes driven to Beirut under extreme conditions. Bargylus takes its name from the Greek name of the mountain range. Christian monasteries and villages also make small amounts of wine and arak.

history.title: The wine of Mari
history.text: Palace archives at Mari record wine supplies and royal requests for fine wine, among the earliest written wine commerce.

history.title: Ugarit's wine trade
history.text: The port city of Ugarit, near Latakia, exported wine and recorded vineyards in its archives.

history.title: Domaine de Bargylus
history.text: The Saadé family planted vineyards in the Jebel Ansariyeh near Latakia and kept producing through the civil war.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Mediterranean coast backed by the Jebel Ansariyeh (Coastal Mountains), with limestone and clay at 800 to 1,000 metres; continental interior plateaus grow table grapes.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
grapes.note: Bargylus's grapes.

grapes.note: Mostly eaten or used for arak.

countries.name: Jordan
countries.tagline: Nabataean presses at Little Petra and two modern wineries on the high plateau.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 3,258 ha of grapes in 2024, mostly table grapes; a few hundred hectares of wine grapes and two main wineries

countries.overview:
Wine in Jordan reaches back to the Nabataeans, whose wine presses and triclinium dining halls at Little Petra (Siq al-Barid) show that grapes were grown and pressed in the desert two thousand years ago, and to the Decapolis city of Gadara (Umm Qais), praised for its wine. The modern industry is tiny but serious. The Haddad family's Eagle Distilleries launched Jordan River Wines (vineyards near Mafraq and Sama as-Sarhan in the north-east, close to the Syrian border), and Omar Zumot's Zumot Winery, best known for its Saint George label, farms organically at Sama as-Sarhan. Vineyards sit at 600 to 850 metres on the basalt-strewn plateau, with very hot days, cold nights and irrigation.

Jordan's Christian minority, around Madaba, Fuheis and Salt, kept a home tradition of wine and arak, and Byzantine church mosaics around Madaba include scenes of grape harvest and treading. The modern wineries sell mostly to hotels and restaurants in Amman and to visitors, and export small quantities.

history.title: Nabataean wine presses at Little Petra
history.text: Rock-cut presses and banquet halls at Siq al-Barid, near Petra, show Nabataean winemaking.

history.title: Modern wineries
history.text: Zumot (Saint George) and Jordan River Wines planted vineyards on the north-eastern plateau near Mafraq.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Arid plateau at 600 to 850 metres near the Syrian border, basalt and limestone soils, drip irrigation essential.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Main varieties.

countries.name: Egypt
countries.tagline: The pharaohs labelled their wine by vintage, estate and winemaker; a modern industry is reviving it on the Nile and by the sea.

stats.note: OIV 2025: 86 kha of vines, almost all table grapes; wine production is small (a few thousand tonnes).

countries.overview:
Egypt gave wine its first labels. The earliest evidence is imported: in tomb U-j at Abydos, built for a ruler of about 3150 BC often identified as Scorpion I, dozens of imported jars held resinated, herb-flavoured wine, and grape seeds, skins and pulp survived alongside them. By the third millennium BC royal vineyards in the Nile Delta made wine for the court and the gods, tomb paintings show the whole process from picking to treading in vats to sealing jars, and wine jars were stamped with the estate's name. The jars in Tutankhamun's tomb (about 1323 BC) carry ink labels giving the regnal year, the estate (often 'of the Western River', in the Delta), the chief vintner's name and whether the wine was red or white; residue analysis showed that some jars held white wine and one held shedeh, a prized red.

Wine was made at the Mareotis lake near Alexandria and in the Western Desert oases (Kharga and Dakhla) through Greek and Roman times, and Christian monasteries kept making it after the Arab conquest. Commercial production collapsed under Islamic rule until 1882, when the Greek-Egyptian tobacco merchant Nestor Gianaclis planted a modern vineyard near Alexandria. Nasser nationalised the industry in 1963, and after privatisation in 1997 the company, Al Ahram Beverages, was bought by Heineken in 2002.

Today a handful of wineries (Gianaclis, Kouroum of the Nile, Egyptian Vineyards, Omar Khayyam) make wine mostly for hotels and the domestic market, from vineyards in the desert near Alexandria and on the Nile near Beni Hasan in Middle Egypt. Kouroum of the Nile has revived the local white grape Bannati. Heat and lack of rain mean every vine is irrigated, and harvests start in July.

history.title: Imported wine in tomb U-j
history.text: A predynastic ruler at Abydos was buried with dozens of imported jars of resinated, herbal wine, among the oldest wine finds in Egypt.

history.title: Royal vineyards of the Delta
history.text: From the Third Dynasty, royal wine estates in the Nile Delta supplied the court; by the end of the Old Kingdom five named wines were a standard offering for the afterlife.

history.title: Tutankhamun's labelled jars
history.text: Wine jars in the boy king's tomb carry dockets naming year, estate, vintner and colour; residue studies identified white wine and the red shedeh.

history.title: The vintage scene in the tomb of Nakht
history.text: The tomb of the scribe Nakht at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna shows grapes picked from a pergola, trodden in a vat and stored in jars, one of the most famous images of ancient winemaking.

history.title: Nestor Gianaclis replants
history.text: A Greek-Egyptian tobacco merchant planted Egypt's first modern vineyard near Alexandria, restarting commercial winemaking.

history.title: Nationalisation and Heineken
history.text: Nasser nationalised wineries and breweries in 1963; the industry was privatised in 1997 and bought by Heineken in 2002.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Desert climate with almost no rain; vineyards on sandy and calcareous soils near the Mediterranean coast and on the Nile valley margins are fully irrigated, and growers use shading and pergolas against the heat.

grapes.note: Local white grape revived by Kouroum of the Nile.

countries.name: Tunisia
countries.tagline: Carthage's wine country, home of the first great agricultural writer and of Cap Bon's dry Muscat.

stats.note: Production: 33,000 t of wine (about 0.33 mhl) in 2022, the latest official figure (FAOSTAT). No official current vineyard total: FAOSTAT's 22,000 to 23,700 ha of grapes for 2022 to 2024 are FAO estimates, and Tunisian press estimates (WMC, July 2026) put the area still worked for wine at about 5,500 to 5,600 ha, against 13,000 ha in 2011, with output down to about 150,000 hl a year

countries.overview:
Tunisia is Carthage, and Carthage wrote the book on viticulture. The Punic agronomist Mago composed a 28-volume treatise on farming, including how to plant and prune vines and how to make passum, raisin wine; when Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, the Senate ordered his work translated into Latin, and Columella, Varro and Pliny quoted it. The Punic town of Kerkouane on Cap Bon, preserved because it was never rebuilt, and Roman villas with wine mosaics (the Bardo museum in Tunis has some of the finest Dionysiac mosaics in the world) show how deeply wine ran through North African life.

After the Arab conquest wine shrank but never vanished, and after the French protectorate began in 1881 large vineyards were planted on the plains around Tunis and on Cap Bon. Seven appellations were created between 1958 and the 1970s and registered internationally under the Lisbon Agreement. Since the late 1990s European investment (from Italy, France and Germany) has modernised a sector that was largely run by state and cooperative wineries.

Tunisian wine is mostly rosé and red from Mediterranean grapes (Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Alicante Bouschet), with dry and sweet Muscat of Alexandria on the windy tip of Cap Bon at Kélibia as the local speciality. The country sells mostly at home, to tourists and to Germany and France.

history.title: Mago's treatise
history.text: The Carthaginian Mago wrote a 28-book agricultural manual, translated into Latin on the Roman Senate's orders after 146 BC; its fragments include advice on vines and raisin wine.

history.title: Kerkouane
history.text: A Punic town on Cap Bon abandoned around 250 BC and never rebuilt, giving a rare picture of Carthaginian domestic life in the Muscat country of Kélibia.

history.title: The French vineyard
history.text: Under the French protectorate large estates were planted around Tunis, Mornag and Cap Bon, mostly for bulk wine shipped to France.

history.title: Tunisia's AOCs
history.text: Muscat de Kélibia and Muscat de Thibar (1958), then Mornag, Coteaux de Tébourba and Sidi Salem (1973) and others were created as appellations.

countries.classification: Tunisia has a French-style system of appellations d'origine contrôlée, with seven names registered under the Lisbon Agreement: Grand Cru Mornag, Mornag, Coteaux de Tébourba, Sidi Salem, Kélibia (Muscat de Kélibia), Thibar (Muscat de Thibar) and Coteaux d'Utique. Labels also use 'Premier Cru' for higher-quality AOC wines.
countries.climate_soils: Mediterranean north and Cap Bon with hot summers and winter rain; sandy and clay-limestone soils; the Atlas foothills around Thibar and Bou Arada are higher and cooler.

grapes.name: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Alicante Bouschet, Merlot
grapes.note: Reds and rosés.

grapes.name: Muscat of Alexandria
grapes.note: Kélibia's grape, dry and sweet.

grapes.name: Chardonnay, Pedro Ximénez, Clairette
grapes.note: Other whites.

countries.name: Algeria
countries.tagline: Once the world's biggest wine exporter, now a quiet producer of sun-baked reds from the hills of Oran and Médéa.

stats.note: OIV 2025: 68 kha of vines (table and wine grapes). Wine production around 500,000 hl in the 2010s (Wein-Plus: 492,000 hl in 2012).

countries.overview:
Algeria's wine story is one of the most dramatic in the world. Phoenicians, Carthaginians and Romans made wine here, and it faded after the Islamic conquest. Then France arrived in 1830, and when phylloxera destroyed French vineyards from the 1860s, settlers planted the Algerian plains and hills on an enormous scale. Production rose from about 25,000 hectolitres in 1854 to 10 million by 1915; by the late 1930s around 400,000 hectares of vines covered the colony, and by around 1960 output reached some 16 million hectolitres. With Morocco and Tunisia, Algeria then accounted for nearly two thirds of the international wine trade, most of it deep-coloured, high-alcohol red shipped to Sète and blended into the thin wines of the Languedoc.

Independence in 1962 broke the system. The pied-noir growers and the French army, the domestic market, left; France sharply cut its purchases; a Soviet contract from 1969 took 500 million litres a year at low prices; and the state, uneasy about depending on alcohol, encouraged growers to replace vines with cereals and table grapes. Within a few decades the wine vineyard shrank to a small fraction of its colonial peak.

Today the state marketing office ONCV (Office National de Commercialisation des Produits Vitivinicoles) dominates production, alongside a few private companies (Grands Crus de l'Ouest and others). Most vineyards lie in the west around Mascara, Tlemcen, Aïn Témouchent and Sidi Bel Abbès, and in the Médéa and Aïn Bessem hills south of Algiers. Seven quality zones survive from the colonial VDQS: Coteaux de Mascara, Coteaux de Tlemcen, Monts du Tessalah, Dahra, Coteaux du Zaccar, Médéa and Aïn Bessem-Bouira. Wines are sturdy reds from Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache and Alicante Bouschet, rosés, and whites from Clairette and Ugni Blanc.

history.title: The great planting
history.text: As phylloxera ravaged France, settlers planted Algeria; production rose from about 25,000 hl to 10 million hl, helped by winemakers from Baden and the south of France.

history.title: Peak vineyard
history.text: About 400,000 ha of vines covered French Algeria, one of the largest vineyards in the world.

history.title: Sixteen million hectolitres
history.text: Algeria produced around 16 million hl and was the world's largest wine exporter, mostly for blending in southern France.

history.title: Independence and collapse
history.text: The departure of settlers and French cuts in imports, then policy favouring cereals, shrank the vineyard dramatically in the following decades.

countries.classification: Seven quality zones (labelled AOG, appellation d'origine garantie) recognised by the ONCV, inherited from French VDQS designations: Coteaux de Mascara, Coteaux de Tlemcen, Monts du Tessalah, Dahra, Coteaux du Zaccar, Médéa and Aïn Bessem-Bouira.
countries.climate_soils: Mediterranean climate on the coastal hills and the Tell Atlas, with about 400 mm of rain in the west and 600 mm in the east; vineyards up to about 1,200 metres around Médéa; clay-limestone and sandy soils.

grapes.name: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet
grapes.note: The historic colonial reds.

grapes.name: Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Newer reds.

grapes.name: Clairette, Ugni Blanc, Merseguera
grapes.note: Whites.

countries.name: Morocco
countries.tagline: The Arab world's leading quality producer, with an AOC in the Atlas foothills and a national love of vin gris.

stats.note: Ministry of Agriculture via FAOSTAT (official figure): 40,032 ha of grapes in 2024, mostly table grapes. OIV data show wine production of 173,000 to 493,000 hl a year between 1995 and 2022, averaging about 355,000 hl (Le Matin, Feb 2026); no official current figure

countries.overview:
Morocco grew vines in Roman times (the ruins of Volubilis, near Meknès, have olive presses and Bacchic mosaics) and again under the French protectorate from 1912, when colonists planted around Meknès, Fès, Rabat and Casablanca. Production peaked above 3 million hectolitres in the 1950s. After independence (1956) the EEC's quotas of 1967 cut exports, and from 1973 the state took over most vineyards; quality fell until the 1990s, when the state company SODEA leased land to foreign investors, mainly French, such as Castel and William Pitters.

The central figure of modern Moroccan wine was Brahim Zniber (about 1920 to 2016), who built Celliers de Meknès and the Diana Holding group into a business that by 2016 controlled about 85 percent of national production and some 8,300 hectares. His Château Roslane, near Meknès, became in 2009 the first estate with 'château' status, and its vineyards make up the country's only AOC, Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru (2001).

Morocco has about 14 AOG zones (appellation d'origine garantie) grouped into five regions, from Berkane and Angad in the east to Guerrouane, Beni M'tir and Zerhoune around Meknès, Zemmour and Zaër near Rabat, and Doukkala inland from El Jadida. Most wine is red, from Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah, but the national style is vin gris, a very pale rosé from Cinsault and Grenache, the best-selling wine in a country where sale to Muslims is technically forbidden and consumption is concentrated in cities, hotels and among tourists. Castel's Boulaouane was for years the best-selling foreign wine in France.

history.title: Roman Volubilis
history.text: The Roman city near Meknès had presses and Bacchic mosaics; the region's wine and oil were traded across the empire.

history.title: The protectorate vineyard
history.text: French settlers planted around Meknès, Fès, Rabat and Casablanca; output passed 3 million hl in the 1950s.

history.title: State control and foreign revival
history.text: The state took over vineyards in 1973; from the 1990s SODEA leased them to French investors.

history.title: Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru
history.text: Morocco's first and only AOC was created for vineyards of Celliers de Meknès around Château Roslane.

countries.classification: Morocco's system, set up from the 1970s and revised in the 1990s and 2000s, has about 14 AOG zones (appellations d'origine garanties) and one AOC, Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru. 'Château' status for single estates was first granted to Château Roslane in 2009.
countries.climate_soils: Mediterranean with Atlantic influence on the coast; the Meknès plateau at 500 to 700 metres and the Middle Atlas foothills are cooler and get 500 to 600 mm of rain. Soils are clay-limestone and sandy; the eastern zones near Berkane are drier.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.note: The most planted wine grape, base of vin gris.

countries.name: Libya
countries.tagline: Greek Cyrene and Roman Leptis drank local wine; production has been banned since 1969.

stats.note: No legal wine production since 1969.

countries.overview:
Libya's coast has two ancient wine landscapes. In the east, Greek colonists from Thera (Santorini) founded Cyrene around 630 BC on the green, rain-fed plateau of the Jebel Akhdar, where vines, olives and grain grew; Cyrenaica traded wine and the famous medicinal plant silphium across the Greek world. In the west, Tripolitania was Punic and then Roman: Leptis Magna, Oea (Tripoli) and Sabratha grew rich on olive oil, and the region also made wine for local use.

Italy took Libya from the Ottomans in 1911 and from the 1930s settled tens of thousands of colonists, who planted vineyards in Tripolitania and on the Jebel Akhdar. After Muammar Gaddafi's coup of 1969 alcohol was banned, and the remaining Italian settlers were expelled in 1970. Libya has had no legal wine industry since, and its grapes are grown for the table.

history.title: Greek Cyrene
history.text: Greek settlers from Thera (Santorini) founded Cyrene and farmed the green Jebel Akhdar, including vines.

history.title: Alcohol banned
history.text: After the revolution of 1969 Libya prohibited alcohol, ending the Italian-era wine industry.

countries.classification: None.
countries.climate_soils: Mediterranean coastal strip; desert inland.

countries.name: Georgia
countries.tagline: Eight thousand years of wine in buried clay jars, from the oldest known vintages on earth to the amber wines that changed modern taste.

stats.note: Vineyard area end of 2024 from the National Statistics Office (Geostat), via FreshPlaza; production 2025 from OIV (largest Georgian harvest in at least 30 years; the National Wine Agency recorded about 336,000 tonnes of grapes processed)

countries.overview:
No country has a better claim to be wine's birthplace. In 2017 a team led by Patrick McGovern and Georgian archaeologists published chemical evidence from pottery jars at two Neolithic villages in Kvemo Kartli, Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, about 50 kilometres south of Tbilisi: tartaric acid, the fingerprint of grapes, along with malic, succinic and citric acids, in vessels dated to roughly 6000 to 5800 BC. That pushed the earliest chemical evidence of grape wine back by several centuries from the Zagros mountains of Iran. Georgians did not need the science to believe it. Wine is woven into the language, the church and the table: St Nino is said to have converted the country in the fourth century with a cross bound from vine branches and her own hair, and a Georgian feast, the *supra*, is run by a *tamada* who proposes toasts for hours.

The heart of the tradition is the *qvevri*, a large egg-shaped clay vessel lined with beeswax and buried up to its neck in the earth of the *marani*, the wine cellar. Crushed grapes go in with their juice, skins, stems and pips, ferment in the ground, and stay sealed on the skins for months. Whites made this way in Kakheti come out deep amber, tannic and savoury, smelling of dried apricot, walnut, tea and honey; this is the style the rest of the world now calls orange wine, and Georgia never stopped making it. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed the traditional qvevri method on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. What is left after pressing, the pomace, becomes *chacha*, the fierce grape spirit served at every celebration.

History has been hard on Georgian vines. Persian and Ottoman invasions repeatedly burned Kakheti: Shah Abbas I's campaigns of 1614 to 1616 depopulated the region and destroyed the royal capital at Gremi. Under Russian rule from 1801 the aristocracy, led by Prince Alexander Chavchavadze at Tsinandali, bottled wine in the European way and started a commercial industry. The Soviet period turned Georgia into the USSR's prestige wine cellar, with semi-sweet Kindzmarauli and Khvanchkara reputedly on Stalin's table, but also into a factory of bulk wine; Gorbachev's 1985 anti-alcohol campaign uprooted vineyards across the republic.

Independence in 1991 brought civil war, poverty and counterfeiting, and in 2006 Russia, then the destination for most Georgian wine, banned it outright, citing quality problems. The embargo lasted until 2013 and forced Georgia to look west. Producers rebuilt around quality, family wineries reopened ancestral *marani*, and a small group of natural winemakers (Pheasant's Tears, Iago Bitarishvili, Ramaz Nikoladze, Okro Natroshvili, Alaverdi Monastery among them) became heroes of the world's natural wine scene. Today Georgia exports wine to about 70 countries, earning around 245 million US dollars from 82 million litres in the first eleven months of 2025, with Russia again the largest buyer by volume and the EU, Poland, the Baltic states, China and the US growing.

The wine map is old and dense. Kakheti, in the east between the Greater Caucasus and the Gombori ridge, grows the great majority of the country's grapes and holds most of the 33 registered appellations of origin, among them Tsinandali, Mukuzani, Kindzmarauli, Napareuli and Gurjaani. Kartli around Tbilisi makes lighter whites and sparkling wine; Imereti in the west uses less skin contact and its own vessel, the *churi*; Racha and Lechkhumi in the mountains produce rare semi-sweet reds. Georgia counts more than 500 indigenous grape varieties, though a few dominate: Rkatsiteli and Saperavi above all, with Kakhuri Mtsvane, Kisi, Khikhvi, Chinuri, Tsolikouri, Tsitska, Aleksandrouli, Mujuretuli, Otskhanuri Sapere and Ojaleshi giving the country's patchwork its colour.

The recent numbers are striking. Georgia's vineyard area grew about 81 percent between the 2014 census and the end of 2024, to roughly 59,900 hectares, and the 2025 harvest, about 336,000 tonnes of grapes processed, was the largest in at least three decades. The OIV puts 2025 wine production at 2.6 million hectolitres. The challenge is to sell that wave of Saperavi and Rkatsiteli at good prices without becoming dependent on a single market again.

history.title: The world's earliest known grape wine
history.text: Pottery jars from the Shulaveri-Shomu villages of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora in Kvemo Kartli held tartaric, malic, succinic and citric acid residues: the earliest chemical evidence of grape wine yet found (McGovern et al., PNAS 2017). A Gadachrili jar also held grape pollen and starch.

history.title: St Nino's cross of vines
history.text: Tradition holds that St Nino, who converted the kingdom of Kartli to Christianity around 337, carried a cross made of grapevine branches tied with her own hair. Vines are carved on the facades of Georgian churches from then on.

history.title: Ikalto: monks, wine and an academy
history.text: Ikalto monastery near Telavi was founded by St Zenon, one of the Thirteen Assyrian Fathers, and became an academy under King David the Builder; its curriculum reportedly included viticulture and winemaking, and a large ancient grape press survives on the site.

history.title: Alaverdi cathedral and its cellar
history.text: The great cathedral of Alaverdi in the Alazani valley dates from the early eleventh century, and its monastic wine cellar from the same era. Restored in 2006, it again makes qvevri wine.

history.title: Shah Abbas devastates Kakheti
history.text: The Safavid shah's campaigns destroyed the Kakhetian royal capital of Gremi, killed or deported a large share of the population and left vineyards abandoned.

history.title: Prince Chavchavadze bottles Georgian wine
history.text: At Tsinandali, the poet and general Alexander Chavchavadze (1786 to 1846) combined European winemaking with Georgian tradition and built what became the country's most famous wine estate; its oenotheque now holds historic bottles dating from 1814.

history.title: Shamil's raid on Tsinandali
history.text: Forces of Imam Shamil raided Tsinandali in July 1854 and took the Chavchavadze princesses hostage; they were exchanged in March 1855 for Shamil's son and 40,000 silver rubles. The estate later passed to the Russian imperial family.

history.title: The Soviet wine cellar
history.text: Georgia became the USSR's prestige wine republic, famous for semi-sweet reds such as Kindzmarauli and Khvanchkara. Vineyards expanded massively, then Gorbachev's 1985 anti-alcohol campaign uprooted large areas.

history.title: The Russian embargo
history.text: Russia, which then took most Georgian wine, banned imports in 2006, officially on quality grounds, amid a political crisis. The ban lasted until 2013 and pushed Georgia towards quality and new markets in Europe, Asia and the Americas.

history.title: UNESCO recognises qvevri winemaking
history.text: The ancient Georgian traditional qvevri winemaking method was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

history.title: Neolithic wine confirmed
history.text: The PNAS paper on Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora was published in November 2017, and the find was named one of Archaeology magazine's top discoveries of the year.

history.title: A record harvest
history.text: About 336,000 tonnes of grapes were processed in the 2025 rtveli (harvest), the largest in at least thirty years, and the appellation list grew with Racha and others to 33 registered PDOs.

countries.classification:
Georgia protects its classic wine names as appellations of origin (PDOs) registered with Sakpatenti, the National Intellectual Property Centre, and controlled by the National Wine Agency. A presidential decree of 2002 listed the first 18 (Tsinandali, Teliani, Napareuli, Vazisubani, Mukuzani, Akhasheni, Gurjaani, Kardenakhi, Tibaani, Kindzmarauli, Manavi, Khvanchkara, Tvishi, Kvareli, Atenuri, Sviri, Kotekhi and Kakheti/Kakhuri), most registered between 2005 and 2007. Since 2018 the list has grown quickly with small microzones applied for by local associations or single wineries: Khashmis Saperavi, Bolnisi, Salkhino Ojaleshi, Akhmeta, Tsarapi, Akhoebi, Magraani Kisi, Zegaani, Okureshis Usakhelouri, Asuretuli Shala, Okami, Obcha, Lechkhumi, Racha and Sazanos Otskhanuri. The National Wine Agency's list stood at 33 by late 2025.

Each appellation fixes a zone, permitted grapes and a style, and the style can be the point: Kindzmarauli, Akhasheni, Khvanchkara and Tvishi are by definition naturally semi-sweet wines, made by chilling the fermentation to leave residual sugar, while Mukuzani and Napareuli are dry reds. 'Kakhuri' (Kakhetian) on a label denotes the traditional Kakhetian method with long skin contact in qvevri; 'Imeruli' (Imeretian) means a lighter maceration with only part of the skins. Georgia also protects Chacha and Georgian brandy as geographical indications, and several PDOs are recognised in the EU under the 2012 EU-Georgia agreement on geographical indications.
countries.climate_soils:
Georgia sits between the Black Sea and the Caspian, sheltered from the north by the Greater Caucasus. The west (Imereti, Samegrelo, Guria, Adjara) is humid and subtropical, with heavy rain and mild winters; the east (Kartli, Kakheti) is drier and more continental, with hot summers and cold winters. Kakheti's main valley, the Alazani, runs north-west to south-east beneath the Caucasus wall, which blocks cold air and sends down cool night breezes; the Iori valley lies across the Gombori ridge to the south-west. Most Kakhetian vineyards sit between about 300 and 800 metres.

Soils change with the rivers: alluvial and brown forest soils in the Alazani valley, carbonate-rich clays and gravels on the right-bank terraces of Mukuzani, Tsinandali and Gurjaani, and red and humus-calcareous soils under Kvareli's Kindzmarauli. Racha's Khvanchkara vineyards climb the steep, limestone-rich slopes of the Rioni gorge around 400 to 750 metres, and Imereti mixes clay, limestone and sandy soils on low hills.

grapes.name: Rkatsiteli
grapes.note: Georgia's most planted white and one of the world's most planted grapes overall; high acidity, made fresh and fruity in steel or amber and tannic in qvevri. Basis of Tsinandali, Gurjaani, Tibaani, Tsarapi and much of Kakheti.

grapes.name: Saperavi
grapes.note: The great red, a teinturier with pink-red flesh: inky, high in acid and tannin, capable of long ageing. Mukuzani, Napareuli, Kvareli and Zegaani are dry Saperavi; Kindzmarauli and Akhasheni are semi-sweet.

grapes.name: Kakhuri Mtsvane
grapes.note: Kakhetian 'green' white: perfumed, mineral; blended with Rkatsiteli in Tsinandali and the main grape of Manavi and Akhmeta.

grapes.name: Kisi
grapes.note: Kakhetian white revived since the 2000s, aromatic and textured, brilliant in qvevri; the grape of Magraani Kisi.

grapes.name: Khikhvi
grapes.note: Rich, aromatic Kakhetian white, traditionally used in fortified Kardenakhi and now made as amber wine.

grapes.name: Chinuri
grapes.note: Kartli's crisp white, used for sparkling Atenuri and for fine amber wines (Iago's Chardakhi).

grapes.name: Goruli Mtsvane
grapes.note: Kartli white, used with Chinuri in Atenuri and Okami.

grapes.name: Tsolikouri
grapes.note: The most planted white of western Georgia; Sviri, Tvishi and Obcha.

grapes.name: Tsitska
grapes.note: High-acid Imeretian white, used for still and sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Krakhuna
grapes.note: Full-bodied Imeretian white, part of Sviri.

grapes.name: Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli
grapes.note: Racha's red pair, the basis of semi-sweet Khvanchkara.

grapes.name: Otskhanuri Sapere
grapes.note: Fiercely tannic Imeretian red, the grape of Obcha (red) and Sazanos Otskhanuri.

grapes.name: Usakhelouri
grapes.note: Rare, perfumed red of Lechkhumi grown on a few hectares; Okureshis Usakhelouri is among Georgia's most expensive wines.

grapes.name: Ojaleshi
grapes.note: Red of Samegrelo and Lechkhumi, traditionally trained up trees; Salkhino Ojaleshi.

grapes.name: Shavkapito, Tavkveri and Asuretuli Shavi
grapes.note: Kartli reds; Asuretuli Shavi grows around Asureti, the former German colony of Elisabethtal, and gives the pale reds of Asuretuli Shala.

countries.name: Armenia
countries.tagline: Home of the world's oldest known winery, Urartian cellars of buried karas jars and a mountain wine revival around Areni.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figures (Statistical Committee of Armenia): 14,384 ha of grapes in 2024 and 14,262 t of wine (about 0.14 mhl) in 2023; most grapes historically went to brandy. Not reported by OIV 2025

countries.overview:
In 2007 archaeologists digging in a three-chambered limestone cave above the Arpa river, near the village of Areni in Vayots Dzor, found a winery: a clay basin about a metre long for treading grapes, sloping to drain juice into a vat about 60 centimetres deep, storage jars, cups, grape seeds, pressed skins and vines, all preserved by the cave's dry air and a layer of sheep dung. Radiocarbon dating placed it around 4100 to 4000 BC, and a 2011 paper by Hans Barnard and colleagues in the Journal of Archaeological Science confirmed malvidin, the pigment of red grapes, in the vessels. Areni-1 is the oldest winery yet found, and the same cave gave the world's oldest leather shoe.

Wine runs through the Urartian kingdom that ruled the Armenian Highlands in the first millennium BC. At Teishebaini (Karmir Blur), a fortress built by King Rusa II on the edge of today's Yerevan, excavators found storerooms with hundreds of karases, huge clay jars sunk into the ground, with capacity marks on their shoulders. Xenophon's Greek army, marching through in 401 BC, was served wine and beer from jars buried in village houses.

Christianity, adopted in 301, kept wine sacred; cross-stones (khachkars) are carved with vines and pomegranates. In the Soviet era Armenia's grapes went mostly into brandy: the Yerevan brandy distillery (founded in 1887, bought by Nikolay Shustov's company in 1899, famous as Ararat brandy and owned by Pernod Ricard since 1998) supplied a quarter of all Soviet brandy, and wine was largely sherry-style or bulk. Since about 2010 a wine renaissance has followed: Zorah (Rind), Trinity Canyon, Old Bridge, Hin Areni, Momik, Voskevaz, ArmAs, Van Ardi, Keush (sparkling at 1,750 metres) and many small producers now bottle native grapes from some of the highest vineyards in the northern hemisphere.

The signature grapes are the red Areni Noir (Areni), thick-skinned, peppery and fresh, grown on its own roots in Vayots Dzor's sandy, volcanic soils at 1,000 to 1,600 metres, and the white Voskehat ('golden berry'), floral and textured. Kangun, a Soviet-era cross, and the red Haghtanak and Sireni (Khndoghni) are also important. The traditional vessel, the karas, is being revived by producers who ferment and age in clay. The Areni Wine Festival, held each October since 2009, celebrates the village's double legacy.

history.title: The Areni-1 winery
history.text: A cave near Areni held a clay treading basin, a fermentation vat, storage jars and domesticated grape remains: the oldest winery yet discovered (Barnard et al. 2011).

history.title: The Areni-1 shoe
history.text: The same cave preserved the world's oldest known leather shoe, found in 2008.

history.title: Erebuni founded
history.text: The Urartian king Argishti I founded the fortress of Erebuni, origin of Yerevan, whose storerooms held wine jars.

history.title: Teishebaini's wine magazines
history.text: Rusa II's fortress at Karmir Blur had storerooms of buried karases; excavations from 1939 found hundreds of jars, many with capacity marks, before its destruction around 585 BC.

history.title: Xenophon's buried jars
history.text: Xenophon's Anabasis describes Armenian villagers storing wine and barley beer in jars sunk into the floors of their houses.

history.title: The Yerevan brandy distillery
history.text: The first brandy factory opened in Yerevan; after Nikolay Shustov's company bought it in 1899 it made Armenian brandy famous across the Russian Empire.

history.title: Excavation and publication of Areni-1
history.text: An Armenian, Irish and American team excavated the cave from 2007; the winery was announced in January 2011.

countries.classification: Armenia has no EU-style appellation system yet. Labels carry the region (Vayots Dzor, Ararat Valley, Aragatsotn, Armavir, Tavush) and the grape; the Vine and Wine Foundation of Armenia promotes the sector, and 'Armenian brandy' is a protected name.
countries.climate_soils: Dry, sunny, continental highland climate with hot summers, very cold winters and big day-night swings; vineyards range from about 800 metres in the Ararat Valley to over 1,700 metres. Soils are volcanic (basalt, tuff), sandy and stony, which kept phylloxera out of much of Vayots Dzor, so many old vines are ungrafted.

grapes.name: Areni Noir
grapes.note: The great native red: medium-bodied, peppery, sour cherry and violet, often ungrafted at high altitude.

grapes.name: Voskehat
grapes.note: The leading native white, floral, apricot and honey.

grapes.name: Kangun
grapes.note: Soviet-era white cross (Rkatsiteli by Sukholimansky), used for wine and brandy.

grapes.name: Haghtanak
grapes.note: Deep-coloured red cross used in blends and dessert wines.

grapes.name: Sireni (Khndoghni)
grapes.note: Red of the Karabakh/Artsakh area, dark and tannic.

grapes.name: Garan Dmak, Chilar, Mskhali, Lalvari, Kakhet
grapes.note: Other native varieties being revived.
