countries.name: Azerbaijan
countries.tagline: German colonists' cellars at Göygöl, the pink Madrasa grape of Shamakhi and a state-backed revival.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figures: 14,233 ha of grapes and 12,720 t of wine (about 0.13 mhl) in 2023. Soviet Azerbaijan harvested about 2 million tonnes of grapes by the early 1980s. Not reported by OIV 2025

countries.overview:
Azerbaijan's wine history is ancient (jars with wine residues of the second millennium BC from Göygöl and Neolithic Kültəpə in Nakhchivan) and recent in equal measure. In 1817 to 1819 Lutheran colonists from Württemberg settled in the South Caucasus with the tsar's permission and founded Helenendorf (today Göygöl) near Ganja and Annenfeld (today Shamkir); families such as the Vohrer brothers and the Hummels built wineries and cognac houses that sold across the Russian Empire. Stalin deported the German community in 1941, but its cellars, including the Göygöl wine plant of 1860, are still in use.

Under the Soviet Union Azerbaijan became one of the biggest grape producers in the USSR, reaching about two million tonnes of grapes by the early 1980s, before Gorbachev's 1985 campaign tore out most of the vines. A state programme from 2012 to 2020 subsidised replanting, and a dozen modern wineries now work in three areas: Ganja and Göygöl, Tovuz and Shamkir in the west, and the Shamakhi and Ismayilli foothills of the Greater Caucasus in the east, where Savalan (Aspi Winery), Chabiant and Meysari make the best-known wines. The local signature is Madrasa (Matrassa), a dark-skinned grape named after the village of Madrasa near Shamakhi, used for deeply coloured dry and sweet reds. Nagorno-Karabakh, internationally recognised as part of Azerbaijan, had Armenian-run wineries (in Hadrut, Martuni and elsewhere, using the local Sireni grape) until the region's ethnic Armenian population left after Azerbaijan's military takeover in September 2023.

history.title: Ancient jars at Göygöl
history.text: Archaeologists found jars with wine remains in the Göygöl district dated to the second millennium BC.

history.title: The Swabian colonies
history.text: Colonists from Württemberg founded Helenendorf (Göygöl) and Annenfeld (Shamkir); their wineries industrialised Azerbaijani wine.

history.title: Deportation of the Germans
history.text: Stalin deported the Caucasus Germans to Central Asia; their cellars passed to Soviet state wineries.

history.title: The vines torn out
history.text: Gorbachev's anti-alcohol campaign destroyed most of Azerbaijan's Soviet-era vineyard.

history.title: State replanting programme
history.text: A national grape and wine programme subsidised new vineyards and wineries such as Savalan, Chabiant and Meysari.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Continental to subtropical, with semi-arid lowlands along the Kura and cooler foothills of the Greater and Lesser Caucasus at 300 to 900 metres; brown and chestnut soils, with winter burying of vines in colder sites.

grapes.name: Madrasa (Matrassa)
grapes.note: Dark local red from Shamakhi, also grown in Georgia and Armenia.

grapes.name: Bayan Shira
grapes.note: Local white, used for still and fortified wines.

grapes.name: Rkatsiteli, Saperavi
grapes.note: Georgian varieties widely planted.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
grapes.note: International varieties in new plantings.

countries.name: Moldova
countries.tagline: The most vine-covered country on earth, where a Soviet wine factory became a nation of underground cities and Fetească.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (total vine area including table grapes and household plots; the national vine register counted about 47,700 ha of commercial wine-grape vineyards in 2024). 2025 output was the highest since 2018.

countries.overview:
Moldova is the country where wine is not a sector of the economy so much as the economy's landscape. Squeezed between Romania and Ukraine, between the Prut and the Dniester, it has about 110,000 hectares of vines on some 33,800 square kilometres, roughly four hectares for every hundred people and the highest density of vineyard per person and per square kilometre of any country. Drive almost any road and the hills are striped with vines; most villages have a cellar, and many families still make their own wine from rows behind the house. Wine and divin, the national brandy, have long been among the country's leading exports.

The history is one of empires using Moldova as their vineyard. Greek colonists on the Black Sea traded wine with the Getae and Dacians; Romans followed. Stephen the Great, prince of Moldavia from 1457 to 1504, is remembered for encouraging viticulture, and medieval Moldavian wine went north to Poland and Russia. After 1812 Bessarabia became part of the Russian Empire, which brought French varieties, German and Swiss colonists and estates such as Purcari (granted its status by Tsar Nicholas I in 1827) and the Mimi family's château at Bulboaca. By 1914 Bessarabia had the largest vineyard area in the Russian Empire. Under the Soviet Union, Moldova was turned into a wine factory: replanting from the 1950s took the vine area to about 220,000 hectares by 1960, and giant state combines shipped sweet and fortified wine, 'Cahor' and sparkling to the whole USSR. Then Gorbachev's anti-alcohol campaign of 1985 to 1987 destroyed about 30 percent of the vineyards.

Independence in 1991 left Moldova dependent on one customer. In 2006 Russia, which took around 80 percent of Moldovan wine, banned it (alongside Georgian wine) for two years; in September 2013, as Moldova prepared to sign its Association Agreement with the EU, Moscow banned it again. Each embargo was a disaster for bulk producers and a turning point for quality. The National Office of Vine and Wine (ONVV) was created in 2013 and launched the national brand Wine of Moldova around the National Wine Day festival, held in Chișinău on the first weekend of October since 2002, and three wine regions were protected as PGIs in the EU in 2016: Codru, Ștefan Vodă and Valul lui Traian, with Divin for brandy.

What a wine nerd finds now is a country with world-class infrastructure built for another age, and a young generation reworking it. Cricova and Mileștii Mici are literally underground cities, carved from the limestone quarries that built Chișinău: Mileștii Mici holds the Guinness record for the largest wine collection, and Cricova's 120 kilometres of streets store sparkling wine and a national collection that includes bottles from Hermann Göring's cellar. Purcari's red blend, Negru de Purcari, was famous in nineteenth-century Europe. Private estates such as Château Vartely, Asconi, Et Cetera, Gitana, Carpe Diem, Fautor, Castel Mimi and Purcari Wineries (listed on the Bucharest stock exchange) export to the EU, the US and China; small producers have doubled their exports of artisanal wine in five years.

The grapes tell two stories. International varieties planted in Russian and Soviet times (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Aligoté, Pinot Noir, Muscat, Rkatsiteli, Saperavi) still dominate. But the native Feteasca family (Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Fetească Neagră) and the red Rară Neagră, along with Moldovan crosses such as Viorica, are the signature now, covering only about a tenth of the vineyard but most of the excitement. Fetească Neagră gives plummy, spicy reds; Rară Neagră is lighter, sour-cherry and floral, and was the original backbone of Negru de Purcari.

The challenge is the vineyard itself. Almost half the registered area is more than 30 years old, and growers have been grubbing up close to 2,000 hectares a year: between 2014 and 2024 about 20,500 hectares were cleared and fewer than 3,900 replanted. Drought and frost hit 2024 hard, before 2025 brought the biggest harvest since 2018 (259,000 tonnes of grapes processed, wine production up about 53 percent). Exports, 144 million litres worth more than 234 million US dollars in 2024, are shifting from bulk to bottle, and from Russia towards Romania, Poland, Ukraine, the EU and even West Africa. In June 2025 Chișinău hosted the OIV World Congress of Vine and Wine for the first time.

history.title: Grape seeds at Vărvăreuca
history.text: Imprints of cultivated grape seeds on pottery from the village of Vărvăreuca, in the north, are among the oldest traces of grape growing between the Prut and the Dniester. Fossil leaves of a prehistoric vine, Vitis teutonica, were found near Naslavcea.

history.title: Stephen the Great's vineyards
history.text: Prince Stephen III of Moldavia promoted viticulture and the import of better varieties; wine became one of medieval Moldavia's main exports to Poland and Russia. His name lives on in the Ștefan Vodă wine region.

history.title: Bessarabia joins the Russian Empire
history.text: The Treaty of Bucharest gave the land between the Prut and the Dniester to Russia. Imperial support, French varieties and colonists from Germany, Switzerland and Bulgaria transformed the vineyard; by 1837 Bessarabia had 14,000 ha of vines.

history.title: Purcari, Bessarabia's first specialised winery
history.text: A decree of Tsar Nicholas I gave Purcari on the Dniester the status of the first specialised winery in Bessarabia. Negru de Purcari later won a gold medal in Paris in 1878 and was served to Queen Victoria and Tsar Nicholas II.

history.title: Constantin Mimi's château
history.text: The Bessarabian statesman and winemaker Constantin Mimi, trained in Montpellier, built a reinforced-concrete winery in the French style at Bulboaca, considered the first château of Bessarabia.

history.title: Phylloxera and recovery
history.text: After phylloxera devastated the vines at the end of the nineteenth century, grafted replanting began in earnest in 1906; by 1914 Bessarabia had the largest vineyard area in the Russian Empire.

history.title: Cricova goes underground
history.text: Limestone galleries dug since the fifteenth century to build Chișinău were turned into Cricova's wine city in the 1950s; Soviet planting took Moldova's vineyard to about 220,000 ha by 1960.

history.title: Mileștii Mici founded
history.text: The state complex for storing and ageing quality wines was set up in the Mileștii Mici galleries south of Chișinău; in 2005 Guinness World Records listed its collection as the largest in the world.

history.title: Gorbachev's anti-alcohol campaign
history.text: Moscow's campaign against drinking led to about 30 percent of Moldova's vineyards being destroyed in two years.

history.title: Russian embargoes
history.text: Russia banned Moldovan wine in 2006 (lifted in 2007 to 2008) and again in September 2013, as Moldova moved to sign its EU Association Agreement. The bans forced a pivot to quality and Western markets.

history.title: Wine of Moldova and the ONVV
history.text: The National Office of Vine and Wine was created and launched the national brand Wine of Moldova, promoted above all at National Wine Day, held on the first weekend of October since 2002.

history.title: EU protection for Codru, Ștefan Vodă and Valul lui Traian
history.text: The three historical wine regions and the brandy name Divin were protected as geographical indications in the EU on 18 October 2016.

history.title: Europe's leaders at Castel Mimi
history.text: Castel Mimi hosted the second summit of the European Political Community on 1 June 2023, a symbol of how far Moldova's wine estates have come.

history.title: The OIV comes to Chișinău
history.text: Moldova hosted the 46th OIV World Congress of Vine and Wine in June 2025 and harvested its biggest crop since 2018.

countries.classification:
Moldova's wine law follows the EU model. At the top are wines with a protected designation of origin (Vin cu Denumire de Origine Protejată, DOP): historic appellations such as Ciumai and Romănești were already protected in the EU before 2016, but PDOs are few and little used on labels. The workhorse is the protected geographical indication (Indicație Geografică Protejată, IGP): Codru in the centre, Ștefan Vodă in the south-east and Valul lui Traian in the south-west, each managed by a growers' association that sets yields, varieties and controls. Divin is a national IGP for wine brandy aged at least three years in oak. Below these sit varietal wines and plain wine.

Older Soviet-era names survive on labels and in cellars: 'Cahor' (a sweet, fortified red in the Russian Orthodox church style, now often called Ciumai or Moldavian dessert wine), 'Negru de Purcari' and 'Roșu de Purcari' (brand names of historic blends) and 'Codru' as a red blend name. Wines labelled IGP must come from registered vineyards in the zone, and the ONVV runs a national vine and wine register.
countries.climate_soils:
Moldova sits around 46 to 48 degrees north, on the same latitude band as Burgundy and Bordeaux, but with a moderately continental climate: hot summers, cold winters (frost below minus 20 degrees C happens), about 400 to 550 mm of rain a year and frequent summer drought. The Black Sea, 60 to 100 kilometres from the south-east, moderates the Ștefan Vodă zone and the Dniester valley, while the Codru hills in the centre are wooded, cooler and wetter, which is why they suit whites and sparkling base wines. The south (Valul lui Traian) is the warmest and driest and gives the ripest reds.

Soils are dominated by chernozem, deep black earths rich in humus and often calcareous, over limestone, loess and clays; the limestone bedrock is what allowed the great underground cellars to be carved. Gentle hills between about 100 and 400 metres give slope and aspect but not much altitude.

grapes.name: Fetească Neagră
grapes.note: The flagship native red: plum, black cherry, spice and smoky notes; made in every style from fresh to oak-aged reserves.

grapes.name: Rară Neagră
grapes.note: Light, aromatic red of the south-east (Romania's Băbească Neagră); the historic backbone of Negru de Purcari.

grapes.name: Fetească Albă
grapes.note: Delicate, floral native white, used for still and sparkling wines; the most planted of the native grapes.

grapes.name: Fetească Regală
grapes.note: A natural cross of Fetească Albă and Grasă de Cotnari: crisp, aromatic, popular for whites and sparkling.

grapes.name: Viorica
grapes.note: Aromatic, disease-resistant Moldovan cross from the 1960s and 1970s, with notes of muscat, basil and lime blossom.

grapes.name: Busuioacă Albă
grapes.note: White Muscat-like variety, aromatic dry and sweet wines.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The leading red, central to Negru de Purcari and most reserve blends.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: Widely planted, soft reds and blends.

grapes.name: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Aligoté and Pinot Gris
grapes.note: The main international whites, used for still and sparkling wine in Codru.

grapes.name: Saperavi and Rkatsiteli
grapes.note: Georgian varieties planted in Soviet times, still common in the south.

grapes.name: Isabella and Lidia
grapes.note: American hybrids grown in home vineyards for traditional village wine, outside the quality categories.

countries.name: Ukraine
countries.tagline: Swiss colonists at Shabo, Golitsyn's sparkling cellars in Crimea and a new generation of winemakers working through war.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figures for government-controlled territory: 26,300 ha of grapes in 2023 and 51,991 t of wine (about 0.52 mhl) in 2022. Before 2014 Ukraine had roughly 50,000 ha of vines including Crimea; occupation of Crimea removed about 17,000 ha and wineries providing about 60 percent of wine, and the war since 2022 has damaged or occupied more vineyards in Kherson, Mykolaiv and Zaporizhzhia

countries.overview:
Ukraine's southern coast has made wine since Greek colonists founded Olbia, Tyras and Chersonesus around the sixth and fifth centuries BC. The modern industry dates from the Russian Empire's conquest of the Black Sea steppe in the late eighteenth century. In 1822, with Alexander I's approval, winegrowers from the Swiss canton of Vaud founded the colony of Chabag, today Shabo, on the Dniester estuary in Bessarabia, and their descendants made wine there until the Second World War. Shabo is again Ukraine's largest wine company, with about 1,200 hectares and a wine culture centre on the old colony.

Crimea was the empire's showcase. Count Mikhail Vorontsov planted the south coast from the 1820s, the Magarach research institute was founded in 1828, and Prince Lev Golitsyn (1845 to 1915) built the sparkling wine cellars of Novy Svet (Noviy Svit), where his wine won at the 1900 Paris exhibition and was renamed for the coronation of Nicholas II, and directed the imperial Massandra winery (1894), whose collection of about a million bottles holds sherries and dessert wines back to 1775. Inkerman near Sevastopol ages wine in old limestone galleries. Crimea is internationally recognised as part of Ukraine; Russia has occupied and claimed it since 2014, and Massandra and other estates now operate under Russian control (the Russian-installed authorities 'nationalised' Massandra and sold it at auction in 2023).

The rest of Ukrainian wine is in the south (Odesa, Mykolaiv and Kherson oblasts) and in Transcarpathia (Zakarpattia) in the west, near Hungary, where Berehove and the Tisza valley have Tokaj-related traditions. Soviet Ukraine was the USSR's largest supplier of wine, with about 250,000 hectares before Gorbachev's 1985 campaign destroyed around 80,000. In the 2010s small producers such as Beykush (on the Berezan estuary near Mykolaiv), Kolonist and 46 Parallel in Odesa, Father and Sons, Chateau Chizay in Transcarpathia and Prince Trubetskoi's estate in Kherson started a quality movement, with local grapes such as Telti-Kuruk and Odessa Black alongside Saperavi, Riesling and Chardonnay.

Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 hit wine country hard. The Prince Trubetskoi estate at Kozatske in Kherson oblast was occupied, looted (including about 32,000 bottles) and its historic chateau destroyed; Artwinery, the sparkling-wine plant at Bakhmut with cellars in old gypsum mines, was forced out and moved production to Odesa; vineyards in Mykolaiv and Zaporizhzhia were mined and shelled. Producers kept harvesting, and exports to the EU have grown.

history.title: Greek colonies on the Black Sea
history.text: Olbia, Tyras (Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi) and Chersonesus made and traded wine; presses and amphorae survive at Chersonesus near Sevastopol.

history.title: The Swiss colony of Chabag
history.text: Vaudois winegrowers led by Louis-Vincent Tardent founded Chabag (Shabo) on the Dniester estuary; their wine was shown at the 1893 Chicago exposition.

history.title: Magarach Institute
history.text: The Russian Empire founded the Magarach viticulture research institute near Yalta; its collection holds thousands of vine varieties.

history.title: Golitsyn's Novy Svet
history.text: Prince Lev Golitsyn developed Novy Svet in Crimea into Russia's first great sparkling wine house and later directed Massandra (founded 1894).

history.title: Anti-alcohol campaign
history.text: About 80,000 ha of Soviet Ukraine's vineyards were destroyed under Gorbachev's campaign.

history.title: Occupation of Crimea
history.text: Russia occupied and annexed Crimea, an annexation not recognised by Ukraine or most of the world; Ukraine lost control of about 17,000 ha of vineyards and the Massandra, Novy Svet and Inkerman wineries.

history.title: Full-scale invasion
history.text: Kherson's Prince Trubetskoi winery was occupied, looted and its chateau destroyed; Bakhmut's Artwinery relocated; southern vineyards were damaged.

countries.classification: Ukraine is building an EU-compatible system of protected geographical indications under its 2019 to 2023 legislation; historic names such as Shabo have been registered nationally. Most labels carry region and grape.
countries.climate_soils: Continental steppe climate moderated by the Black Sea in the south, with hot dry summers and cold winters (vines are sometimes buried); chernozem and southern chernozem on loess. Transcarpathia is wetter and volcanic. Crimea's south coast is sub-Mediterranean, protected by the Crimean Mountains.

grapes.name: Telti-Kuruk
grapes.note: Aromatic local white of the Budjak (southern Bessarabia).

grapes.name: Odessa Black (Alibernet)
grapes.note: Soviet-era teinturier cross of Alicante Bouschet and Cabernet Sauvignon.

grapes.name: Saperavi, Rkatsiteli, Aligoté
grapes.note: Soviet-era staples.

grapes.name: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: International varieties.

grapes.name: Sukholimansky White
grapes.note: Odesa cross (Chasselas by Plavai).

countries.name: Russia
countries.tagline: Imperial sparkling at Abrau-Durso, the Don Cossacks' native reds and a protected, fast-growing domestic industry.

stats.note: OIV 2025 (figures as reported by Russia, including occupied Crimea and Sevastopol, which are internationally recognised as Ukraine).

countries.overview:
Most of Russia is too cold for vines, but its south, along the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and the Caspian, has a wine history as old as anyone's. Greek colonies on the Taman peninsula (Phanagoria, Gorgippia at today's Anapa) made wine in the sixth century BC. The Don Cossacks grew vines on the river's islands and terraces from the seventeenth century and kept their own red grapes, Tsimlyansky Cherny, Krasnostop Zolotovsky and Plechistik; the sparkling red Tsimlyanskoye was praised by Pushkin.

In 1870 Tsar Alexander II founded an imperial estate at Abrau-Durso, by a mountain lake near Novorossiysk, and in 1891 Prince Lev Golitsyn, already famous for Crimea's Novy Svet, took charge and brought French specialists to make sparkling wine by the traditional method. The Soviet Union turned Abrau-Durso into the model for 'Sovetskoye Shampanskoye', most of which was made by the tank method in giant plants. Gorbachev's 1985 campaign destroyed much of the vineyard.

Since the 2000s private investment has rebuilt Kuban (Krasnodar Krai), now the heart of Russian wine, with the Taman peninsula, Anapa and the Krymsk-Abrau area: Fanagoria, Kuban-Vino (Château Tamagne), Lefkadia, Gai-Kodzor, Château le Grand Vostock, Abrau-Durso (now a listed company and Russia's largest sparkling wine producer) and many small estates. The Don valley in Rostov oblast, Stavropol and Dagestan (Derbent) add native grapes and brandy. A federal law on viticulture and winemaking in force from June 2020 reserved 'Russian wine' for wine from Russian grapes and set up protected geographical indications (ZGU) and protected designations of origin (ZNMP). Approved geographical names include Kuban, Kuban. Taman Peninsula, Don Valley, Stavropol, Dagestan, Terek Valley, Lower Volga and Crimea; by 2020 there were 15 ZGU and 23 ZNMP, with more since. Import duties on wine from countries Russia designates 'unfriendly' rose to 20 percent in 2023 and 25 percent in 2024, handing domestic producers a protected market. Production reached 5.7 million hectolitres in 2025.

history.title: Phanagoria and Gorgippia
history.text: Greek colonists on the Taman peninsula and at Gorgippia (Anapa) grew vines and traded wine; ancient presses have been excavated.

history.title: Cossack wines of the Don
history.text: Don Cossack stanitsas such as Tsimlyanskaya and Razdorskaya grew native red grapes; sparkling Tsimlyanskoye was praised by Pushkin.

history.title: Imperial Abrau-Durso
history.text: Tsar Alexander II founded an imperial estate at Abrau-Durso on 25 November 1870 to supply the court.

history.title: Golitsyn makes champagne for the tsar
history.text: Prince Lev Golitsyn, appointed head of the imperial vineyards, brought French winemakers to Abrau-Durso; by 1897 it held over 13,000 bottles of sparkling wine in its cellars.

history.title: Anti-alcohol campaign
history.text: Gorbachev's campaign uprooted vineyards across southern Russia.

history.title: Federal wine law
history.text: Law 468-FZ on viticulture and winemaking came into force on 26 June 2020, reserving 'Russian wine' for domestic grapes and setting up ZGU and ZNMP designations.

countries.classification: Since the 2020 law, Russian wine can carry a protected geographical indication (ZGU, roughly an IGP: Kuban, Kuban. Taman Peninsula, Don Valley, Stavropol, Dagestan, Terek Valley, Lower Volga and others) or a protected designation of origin (ZNMP, smaller zones often tied to one estate, especially in Krasnodar Krai). 'Russian wine' requires 100 percent Russian-grown grapes; wine made from imported bulk or concentrate must say so. Russia also lists Crimea and Sevastopol as geographical indications, which Ukraine and most states regard as occupied Ukrainian territory.
countries.climate_soils: Continental, with harsh winters in Rostov, Stavropol and Dagestan where vines are buried for protection; the Black Sea coast around Anapa, Taman and Novorossiysk is milder. Soils range from chernozem to marl, limestone and the sandy islands of the Don.

countries.name: Kazakhstan
countries.tagline: Vineyards under the Tian Shan east of Almaty, where a young estate industry buries its vines each winter.

stats.note: Bureau of National Statistics via FAOSTAT (official figure): 9,551 ha of grapes in 2024, mostly table grapes; FAOSTAT's official series also records about 26,000 t of wine a year in 2022 and 2023

countries.overview: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country, but almost all of it is too cold or too dry for vines. Its wine country lies in the far south-east, in the foothills of the Zailiysky Alatau (Tian Shan) east of Almaty, and in the south around Shymkent and the Turkestan region. Soviet planners established large vineyards here; many were lost after 1985 and 1991. Since the late 2000s private estates have replanted the Almaty region, most visibly Arba Wine in the Enbekshikazakh district towards Shelek and Turgen, with others nearby. Winters are severe enough that vines are buried in autumn and dug out in spring, and summers are hot and dry with irrigation from mountain rivers. Kazakhstan is also an important market for Georgian and Moldovan wine.

history.title: State vineyards in the south
history.text: Soviet planners planted vineyards in the Almaty and Shymkent regions, many of them lost after the 1985 anti-alcohol campaign and independence.

history.title: Private estates east of Almaty
history.text: New wineries such as Arba Wine replanted the foothills east of Almaty.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Extreme continental, 600 to 1,000 metres, vines buried in winter, irrigated loess and alluvial fans.

grapes.name: Saperavi, Rkatsiteli, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Chardonnay
grapes.note: Main varieties.

countries.name: Uzbekistan
countries.tagline: A vast Silk Road vineyard of table grapes and raisins, with Samarkand's nineteenth-century winery still making sweet fortified wines.

stats.note: OIV 2025: 125 kha of vines, the 14th largest vineyard area in the world, overwhelmingly table grapes and raisins; wine output small and not reported.

countries.overview:
Grapes have grown in the oases of Transoxiana for thousands of years. Chinese envoys of the Han dynasty described the wine of Ferghana in the second century BC, Sogdian merchants carried wine and vines along the Silk Road, and Samarkand and Bukhara were famous for their grapes long after Islam made wine a matter of poetry rather than commerce.

The modern industry arrived with the Russian Empire. In Samarkand, a winery founded in 1868 according to its own history by the merchant D. M. Filatov became, in Soviet times, the Khovrenko winery, named after the oenologist M. A. Khovrenko, who led it and developed its range. It is known for sweet and fortified wines in the Soviet style, such as Gulyakandoz, Shirin and Aleatiko, made from grapes grown in a hot continental climate with very high sugar, and for its museum and tasting room. In the Soviet era Uzbekistan was a major source of dessert wines and brandy for the USSR.

Today Uzbekistan has one of the world's largest vineyards by area (about 125,000 hectares, the 14th largest according to the OIV), but almost all of it is for table grapes and raisins, and the wine sector is small. Since the late 2010s the government has opened the economy and encouraged private wineries and wine tourism around Tashkent (Parkent, Bostanliq) and Samarkand.

history.title: Ferghana's wine and the Han envoys
history.text: Chinese envoy Zhang Qian reported that the people of Ferghana made wine from grapes and stored it for years; the Han court brought vines back to China.

history.title: Filatov's Samarkand winery
history.text: A winery was founded in Samarkand, according to its own history, by the merchant D. M. Filatov, shortly after the Russian conquest of the city.

history.title: Khovrenko and Uzbek dessert wines
history.text: Under the oenologist M. A. Khovrenko the Samarkand winery developed sweet and fortified wines that won medals across the USSR; it now bears his name.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Hot, dry continental desert-oasis climate with very hot summers, cold winters (vines are often buried) and irrigation from mountain rivers; loess and alluvial soils.

grapes.note: Soviet-era wine grapes.

grapes.name: Kattakurgan, Husayne, Kishmish
grapes.note: Local table and raisin grapes.

countries.name: Tajikistan
countries.tagline: Sogdian Panjakent's ancient presses and a small Soviet-era wine legacy.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 35,800 ha of grapes in 2023, mostly table grapes and raisins; wine production minimal

countries.overview:
Tajikistan's claim on wine history lies in Sogdiana, the land of the Silk Road's great merchants. The Sogdian city of Panjakent in the Zeravshan valley, abandoned after the Arab conquest in the eighth century, has yielded wine presses, storage jars and painted banquet halls, evidence of a flourishing pre-Islamic wine culture shared with Samarkand, 60 kilometres downstream. The northern Sughd region around Khujand also reaches into the Ferghana valley, the ancient kingdom of Dayuan whose wine impressed Chinese envoys in the second century BC.

In Soviet times the Hissar valley west of Dushanbe and the Ferghana fringe around Khujand had state vineyards and wineries producing dessert wines and brandy. Since independence and the civil war of the 1990s, grape growing has shifted overwhelmingly to table grapes and raisins, and wine production is small and aimed at the domestic market. Hot, dry summers, cold winters and irrigation from mountain rivers define the vineyards.

history.title: Sogdian Panjakent
history.text: The Sogdian merchant city had wine presses and painted banquet halls before the Arab conquest.

countries.classification: No appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Hot continental valleys under high mountains; irrigated.

grapes.name: Rkatsiteli, Saperavi, local table grapes
grapes.note: Main varieties.

countries.name: Kyrgyzstan
countries.tagline: A few vineyards in the Chui and Issyk-Kul valleys and the Ferghana fringe.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 2,645 ha of grapes in 2024 (4,117 ha in 2023); very small wine production

countries.overview:
Kyrgyzstan is mountain country, almost entirely above 1,000 metres, and grapes grow only on its edges. In the south, the Kyrgyz part of the Ferghana valley around Osh and Jalal-Abad belongs to one of the oldest grape-growing areas of Central Asia: Ferghana was the kingdom of Dayuan, whose grape wine the Han envoy Zhang Qian reported in the second century BC, and whose vines were carried back to China. In the north, the Chui valley around Bishkek and the shores of Lake Issyk-Kul, a huge high lake that softens the local climate, had Soviet-era vineyards and wineries that made fortified and fruit wines for the USSR.

Most of those vineyards were lost after the anti-alcohol campaign of 1985 and independence in 1991, and today Kyrgyzstan makes little grape wine; much of what is sold locally is fruit wine or imported. The continental climate, with very cold winters, means vines must be buried each autumn, as across most of Central Asia.

countries.name: Turkmenistan
countries.tagline: Parthian Nisa's wine archive and Soviet desert vineyards.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 19,995 ha of grapes in 2024, mostly table grapes; small state-run wine production with no reliable output data

countries.overview:
Turkmenistan is mostly desert, the Karakum, but its southern oases along the Kopet Dag mountains and the Murghab river were centres of civilisation for thousands of years. At Old Nisa, near Ashgabat, the early Parthian royal fortress (from about the third century BC) yielded more than 2,000 inscribed potsherds, written in Aramaic script, that are largely receipts for wine delivered from royal and temple vineyards to the stores: one of the great administrative wine archives of antiquity, showing a state that taxed and tracked wine by vintage and estate. Merv, in the Murghab oasis, was one of the great cities of the Silk Road.

In Soviet times Turkmenistan grew grapes in the Kopet Dag foothills and the Murghab and Amu Darya oases, and state wineries made dessert wines and brandy. Today grapes are grown mostly for eating, and a small state-controlled industry produces wine for the domestic market. Summers are extremely hot and all vineyards are irrigated.

countries.name: Iran
countries.tagline: Neolithic resinated wine in the Zagros and the wine poetry of Hafez; production banned since 1979.

stats.note: OIV 2025: 128 kha of vines, all for table grapes and raisins (Iran is a major raisin producer). Commercial wine production has been illegal since the 1979 revolution; licensed religious minorities may make wine for their own use.

countries.overview:
Iran holds some of the oldest evidence of wine in the world. At Hajji Firuz Tepe, a Neolithic village in the Zagros mountains south of Lake Urmia excavated by the Penn Museum in 1958 to 1968, six jars of about nine litres each, set into the floor of a mudbrick house of about 5400 to 5000 BC, held residues of tartaric acid and terebinth resin: a resinated wine, published by Patrick McGovern in Nature in 1996 and for two decades the oldest chemical evidence of grape wine. At Godin Tepe, further south, jars of about 3100 to 2900 BC with red residue and wine stains on their sides (they were stored lying down) show a trade in wine along the routes to Mesopotamia.

Persian kings feasted on wine at Persepolis, and wine remained central to court culture and poetry after Islam. The ghazals of Hafez of Shiraz (fourteenth century) and the quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam made wine the great metaphor of mystical love, and Shiraz, in Fars province, was renowned for its wine into the twentieth century; European travellers such as Jean Chardin described it in the seventeenth. The Syrah grape is sometimes said to come from Shiraz, but DNA has shown it is a cross of two French varieties from the Rhône. Before 1979 Iran had a few hundred wineries; after the revolution commercial alcohol was banned, and Iran's vineyards today grow table grapes and raisins (Takestan near Qazvin and Malayer are major raisin centres).

countries.name: Iraq
countries.tagline: Mesopotamia's beer country, where wine was the imported luxury of kings.

stats.note: No significant modern wine production; Christian villages in the north make small amounts.

countries.overview:
In ancient Mesopotamia beer was the everyday drink and wine an expensive import. The alluvial plains of Sumer and Babylonia were too hot, flat and salty for good vines, so wine came down the Tigris and Euphrates from the hills of the north and from Syria and the Zagros; Sumerian texts call it the beer of the mountains. The trade route that ran past Godin Tepe in the Zagros carried wine to the lowland cities by the late fourth millennium BC.

Royal archives show wine as a palace luxury. At Mari on the Euphrates, letters of the eighteenth century BC discuss wine shipments; at Nimrud (Kalhu), the Assyrian capital, the so-called wine lists of the eighth century BC record rations for the royal household and staff; and a famous relief from Nineveh shows King Ashurbanipal and his queen drinking wine beneath a grapevine, with the severed head of an enemy king hanging nearby. The hills of northern Iraq, in today's Kurdistan region, had vineyards in Assyrian times.

Today Iraq has no notable wine industry. Assyrian and Chaldean Christian villages around Alqosh and in the Nineveh plains make small amounts of wine and arak for church and home.

regions.name: Macedonia
regions.tagline: Xinomavro country: cool mountain slopes, lakes and Greece's most age-worthy reds.
regions.summary: Northern Greece's largest wine region stretches from the lakes of Florina and Amyndeon in the west to Drama and Kavala in the east. Its spine is Xinomavro, the grape behind Naoussa, Amyndeon, Goumenissa and (just over the border in Thessaly) Rapsani, but the region also launched modern Greek white wine at Epanomi and Drama and hosts the historic estate of Domaine Carras on Halkidiki.
regions.history: Macedonian wine was praised in antiquity, and Naoussa was already a merchant town making wine in Ottoman times; Boutari was founded there in 1879. Phylloxera arrived in 1898 and destroyed much of the region before replanting on American rootstock. The 1990s brought a cluster of ambitious estates: Kir-Yianni (Naoussa and Amyndeon), Alpha Estate (Amyndeon), Gerovassiliou and Biblia Chora (Epanomi and Kavala), Pavlidis and Wine Art (Drama), and the Thymiopoulos family's biodynamic work at Trilofo.
regions.terroir: Continental influence and altitude set the tone. Mount Vermio shelters Naoussa; Amyndeon sits at 570 to 750 metres around four lakes that moderate frost; Goumenissa lies on the slopes of Mount Paiko. Soils range from marl and limestone to sand, and sandy pockets in Amyndeon still hold ungrafted vines.
regions.grapes: Xinomavro dominates the reds, with Negoska in Goumenissa; Malagousia, Assyrtiko and Sauvignon Blanc lead whites at Epanomi and Drama; Limnio and international varieties grow on Halkidiki.
regions.styles: Structured dry reds, Blanc de Noirs and rosé sparkling Xinomavro in Amyndeon, aromatic whites, and modern Bordeaux-style blends under PGI Drama and PGI Macedonia.
regions.classification: PDOs: Naoussa, Amyndeon, Goumenissa, Slopes of Meliton. Much of the region's best white wine is PGI (Epanomi, Drama, Macedonia).

regions.name: Peloponnese
regions.tagline: Greece's biggest wine region: Nemea's reds, Mantinia's aromatic whites and the sweet wines of Patras.
regions.summary: The Peloponnese makes roughly a quarter of Greek wine and holds seven PDOs. regions.name: Kakheti
regions.tagline: The Alazani valley under the Caucasus wall: Saperavi, Rkatsiteli and amber wine.
regions.summary: Kakheti is to Georgian wine what Bordeaux is to French: the source of most of the country's grapes (about 327,000 of the 336,000 tonnes processed in 2025) and of 20 or more of its 33 appellations. Traditionally it is divided into Inner Kakheti (Shida Kakheti), along both banks of the Alazani river around Telavi, Gurjaani, Kvareli and Sighnaghi, and Outer Kakheti (Gare Kakheti), the drier land around Sagarejo and the Iori valley where Manavi and Khashmi lie. This is the home of the Kakhetian method: grapes, skins, stems and pips fermented and macerated together in qvevri for up to six months, giving amber whites and tannic Saperavi.
regions.history: The kingdom of Kakheti (1465 to 1762) had its capital at Gremi, destroyed by Shah Abbas I in 1616. Monasteries such as Alaverdi, Ikalto, Shuamta and Nekresi kept winemaking alive through invasion. In the nineteenth century the Chavchavadze family at Tsinandali, the Andronikashvili family at Kardenakhi and the Russian imperial Udel (appanage) estates at Napareuli and Tsinandali built the commercial wine industry. In Soviet times giant state wineries in Telavi, Gurjaani and Kvareli made the semi-sweet wines Moscow loved.
regions.terroir: The Greater Caucasus rises to over 4,000 metres immediately north of the Alazani valley, shielding it from Arctic air and draining cool air down at night. Vineyards lie between about 250 and 800 metres. Right-bank sites (Tsinandali, Mukuzani, Gurjaani, Vazisubani) sit on terraces of carbonate-rich alluvium and clay; left-bank sites (Kvareli, Kindzmarauli, Napareuli) are closer to the mountains on deeper, often red, soils. Hail and spring frost are real risks.
regions.grapes: Rkatsiteli and Saperavi dominate; Kakhuri Mtsvane, Kisi, Khikhvi, Saperavi Budeshuri, Cabernet Sauvignon (Teliani) and many rare varieties also grow.
regions.styles: Dry and semi-sweet reds, fresh European-style whites, amber qvevri whites, fortified Kardenakhi.
regions.classification: PDOs: Tsinandali, Mukuzani, Kindzmarauli, Napareuli, Gurjaani, Akhasheni, Manavi, Vazisubani, Teliani, Kardenakhi, Kotekhi, Tibaani, Kvareli, Kakheti, Khashmis Saperavi, Akhmeta, Tsarapi, Akhoebi, Magraani Kisi, Zegaani.

regions.name: Kartli
regions.tagline: Around Tbilisi: Neolithic wine villages, Chinuri and Georgia's sparkling tradition.
regions.summary: Kartli, the historical core of the Georgian kingdom along the Mtkvari (Kura) river, is cooler and windier than Kakheti and makes lighter whites, rosés and sparkling wine. Kvemo Kartli (Lower Kartli) in the south holds the Neolithic sites of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora and the appellations Bolnisi and Asuretuli Shala; Shida Kartli (Inner Kartli) around Gori holds Atenuri and Okami; the Mukhrani valley near Mtskheta is home to Château Mukhrani and Iago Bitarishvili's Chinuri.
regions.history: Ateni's Sioni church (seventh century) stands above the Atenuri vineyards. Prince Ivane Mukhranbatoni founded the Mukhrani estate in the 1870s and exported wine to Europe. German settlers from Württemberg founded colonies in Kvemo Kartli in the 1810s (Katharinenfeld, now Bolnisi; Elisabethtal, now Asureti) and planted vineyards; they were deported in 1941.
regions.terroir: Continental climate, 500 to 800 metres, colder winters than Kakheti; soils of alluvium, gravel and carbonate clay.
regions.grapes: Chinuri, Goruli Mtsvane, Shavkapito, Tavkveri, Asuretuli Shavi, Rkatsiteli, Saperavi.
regions.styles: Light and sparkling whites, rosé-style reds, delicate amber Chinuri.
regions.classification: PDOs: Atenuri, Okami, Bolnisi, Asuretuli Shala.

regions.tagline: Western Georgia's gentler way: churi jars, less skin and bright Tsolikouri.
regions.summary: Imereti, in the humid west around Kutaisi, makes wine in the same buried clay vessels (here called churi) but with only a part of the skins and no stems, so whites are lighter and fresher than Kakhetian amber wines. regions.name: Codru
regions.tagline: Forested central hills, underground cities and Moldova's whites and sparkling wines.
regions.summary: Codru, meaning 'forest' in Romanian, is the central wine region around Chișinău, Strășeni, Orhei, Ialoveni and Hîncești, and the largest of the three IGPs (around 60,000 ha of vineyard by Wine of Moldova's count). Château Vartely, Asconi, Château Cojușna, Carpe Diem and Gitana are among the leading estates.

regions.terroir: Hills of 200 to 400 metres with forest cover, grey forest soils and leached chernozem over limestone; about 550 mm of rain.

regions.styles: Crisp whites, traditional-method sparkling, lighter reds.

appellations.name: Santorini
appellations.grapes: Assyrtiko (at least 75% for dry white), Athiri, Aidani; Vinsanto mostly Assyrtiko with Aidani
appellations.summary:
Santorini makes the most distinctive white wine in Greece and one of the most distinctive anywhere. The island is the rim of a collapsed volcano: the Bronze Age eruption that buried Akrotiri left a blanket of ash and pumice with almost no organic matter and no clay, and on it grows Assyrtiko, a grape that keeps searing acidity under a hot sun. Dry Santorini (at least 75% Assyrtiko, the rest Athiri and Aidani) tastes of lemon, flint and sea spray, gains weight and smoky complexity with age, and is the reason Assyrtiko is now planted from Macedonia to South Australia.

Two traditional styles carry the island's history. Nykteri, from 'night work', was originally picked and pressed at night to avoid the heat; today it is a richer, oak-aged dry white. Vinsanto, the island's sweet wine (the name probably means 'wine of Santorini', not 'holy wine'), is made from grapes dried in the sun for around two weeks and aged at least two years in oak, giving a dark, figgy, acid-lit dessert wine that can outlive its makers.

Scarcity is part of the story. The island has about 1,200 hectares of vines, shrinking under hotels and villas, and yields are tiny: drought, wind and old vines often give a fraction of the legal limit, and the 2023 and 2024 crops were painfully small. Prices for top bottlings have risen sharply.
appellations.terroir: No clay means no phylloxera, so vines grow on their own roots, some root systems claimed to be centuries old; growers periodically cut the old trunk away and let a new shoot grow from the same roots. The vines are trained low as kouloures, baskets woven from the canes, with the grapes hanging inside, out of the wind and sun. Night humidity from the sea is absorbed by the porous pumice and keeps unirrigated vines alive through summers with almost no rain. Sub-zones such as Pyrgos, Megalochori, Akrotiri, Oia and Imerovigli give perceptibly different wines, and producers now bottle them separately.
appellations.nerd_note: The basket vines are rewoven every winter and can be 'rejuvenated' by cutting back to the root, so a vine's above-ground part may be young while its roots are hundreds of years old.

appellations.name: Naoussa
appellations.summary:
Naoussa is the home of Xinomavro and Greece's most serious red wine appellation. The town sits on the eastern flank of Mount Vermio, and its vineyards run along the slopes at roughly 150 to 450 metres, with Kir-Yianni, Thymiopoulos, Dalamara, Karydas, Chrisohoou and the founding house of Boutari (1879) at the core of the local tradition. The wine must be pure Xinomavro, a grape whose name means 'acid-black' though it is rarely black: in the glass Naoussa is translucent garnet, with high acidity, firm tannins and a perfume of sour cherry, tomato leaf, olive, dried rose and spice that develops towards leather and forest floor over ten to twenty years.

The comparison with Barolo is inevitable and partly fair. Like Nebbiolo, Xinomavro is sensitive to site and vintage, slow to reveal itself and unforgiving of over-extraction. The modern debate in Naoussa mirrors Piedmont's: large old casks versus new oak, early drinking versus long ageing, single-vineyard bottlings versus blends of villages. Growers increasingly name their sites, from Trilofo and Fytia in the south to Gastra, Yianakochori and Ramnista.
appellations.terroir: Mount Vermio shelters the vineyards from cold north-westerly winds and drains cool air down the slopes at night. Soils vary from marl and clay to limestone and sandy loam; sandier sites give lighter, more perfumed wines, clay sites darker, firmer ones. The continental climate gives cold winters and warm summers with a long autumn.
appellations.nerd_note: Kir-Yianni was founded in 1997 by Yiannis Boutaris, who left his family firm to make site-driven Xinomavro; he later became mayor of Thessaloniki.

appellations.name: Amyndeon
appellations.summary: The coolest PDO in Greece sits on a high plateau in western Macedonia at 570 to 750 metres, around the lakes Vegoritida, Petron, Zazari and Chimaditida. That altitude and the lakes' moderating effect make Amyndeon the natural home of sparkling and rosé Xinomavro as well as fresher, more aromatic reds than Naoussa's. It is also one of the few PDOs in Greece that allows rosé and sparkling wine.
appellations.terroir: Sandy soils in parts of the zone resisted phylloxera, so some ungrafted old Xinomavro survives. Frost and a short season are the risks.
appellations.nerd_note: Alpha Estate's ungrafted Xinomavro block 'Hedgehog' sits on sandy soil near the lake.

appellations.name: Goumenissa
appellations.summary: On the lower slopes of Mount Paiko north-west of Thessaloniki, Goumenissa blends Xinomavro with the softer, deeply coloured Negoska. The result is rounder and earlier-drinking than Naoussa but keeps Xinomavro's spice and acidity. Small family estates dominate.
appellations.terroir: Paiko's foothills at 200 to 400 metres, sandy clay and limestone, a more open, slightly warmer position than Naoussa.
appellations.nerd_note: Negoska is grown almost nowhere else; its name probably comes from the old Slavic name of Naoussa.

appellations.name: Rapsani
appellations.summary: Rapsani is the Mount Olympus appellation, a historic field blend of Xinomavro with two local grapes, Krassato and Stavroto, grown on the mountain's south-eastern slopes above the Tempi valley. Tsantali revived it from 1991 and still dominates; the wines are spicy, medium-bodied and grow more refined as the vineyards climb.
appellations.terroir: Schist soils between about 300 and 700 metres on Olympus, with the Aegean a few kilometres east. Producers distinguish lower, middle and upper zones.
appellations.nerd_note: Tsantali's Rapsani Grande Reserve comes from the highest, schist-rich parcels, which locals call the 'old vines of the gods'.

appellations.name: Slopes of Meliton
appellations.grapes: Red: Limnio with Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc; white: Athiri, Roditis, Assyrtiko
appellations.summary: A one-estate appellation on the Sithonia peninsula of Halkidiki, created for Domaine Porto Carras, which John Carras planted from the 1960s with advice from Émile Peynaud. Its red blend of Limnio and Cabernet was the first Greek appellation to include international varieties, and the estate trained a generation of Greek winemakers, including Evangelos Gerovassiliou.
appellations.terroir: Granite and schist slopes above the sea on Mount Meliton (Itamos).
appellations.nerd_note: Malagousia's rescue began here: Professor Vassilis Logothetis collected the near-extinct vine and Gerovassiliou propagated it at Porto Carras before planting it at Epanomi.

appellations.name: Anchialos
appellations.summary: A small white-wine PDO on the shore of the Pagasetic Gulf near Volos, blending Roditis and Savatiano into fresh, lemony wines for local fish tavernas. Most production is cooperative. The wines are light, crisp and meant for drinking young, with Roditis giving citrus freshness and Savatiano a little more body.
appellations.terroir: Flat to gently sloping coastal land with sea breezes; light, calcareous soils.

appellations.name: Mesenikola
appellations.grapes: Mavro Messenikola with Carignan and Syrah
appellations.summary: Named after a village near Lake Plastiras in the foothills of the Agrafa mountains, this PDO is built around the rare local Mavro Messenikola, softened with Carignan and Syrah. The wines are light, peppery reds; very little leaves the region.
appellations.terroir: Hillside vineyards above the Thessalian plain at around 200 to 500 metres.

appellations.name: Zitsa
appellations.summary: In the mountains north of Ioannina, Zitsa makes still and lightly sparkling white wine from Debina, a high-acid grape with apple and white-flower aromas. The semi-sparkling style is traditional, and the region was praised by Byron, who stayed at the monastery of Profitis Ilias in 1809.
appellations.terroir: Around 600 metres, high rainfall, cool nights, clay-limestone soils. Grapes ripen late and keep low alcohol.
appellations.nerd_note: Debina is one of very few Greek grapes routinely made as a pétillant wine in a traditional regional style.

appellations.name: Nemea
appellations.summary:
Nemea is Greece's largest red wine appellation and the home of Agiorgitiko (St George's grape). It covers 17 villages in the hills of Korinthia, plus two (Gymno and Malandreni) in north-western Argolida, making it the only Greek PDO spread across two prefectures. Agiorgitiko is the Merlot of Greece in its generosity: soft tannins, plum, cherry and sweet spice, but with enough freshness at altitude to age well. Styles range from fresh, fruity reds to oak-aged reserves and rarer semi-sweet, fortified and sun-dried sweet wines; rosé and blends are made but must be labelled as PGI.

The appellation links itself to the ancient Phliasian wine and to the myth of Heracles and the Nemean lion; locals still call the wine 'blood of Hercules'. The Temple of Zeus at Ancient Nemea stands among the vines.
appellations.terroir: Vineyards climb from about 230 metres on the valley floor to around 850 metres. Producers talk of three altitude bands: a low zone (Nemea, Ancient Nemea, Ancient Kleones, Leontio, Gymno) of richer red clay; a middle zone (Koutsi, Dafni) widely considered the sweet spot for structured reds; and a high zone (Asprokampos, Psari, Kastraki, Kefalari and others) of cooler, stonier sites that give fresher wines. These sub-zones are informal and not codified in the PDO rules; proposals to formalise them have been discussed for years.
appellations.nerd_note: Koutsi has the reputation of a grand cru, and wines from it often carry the village name in fantasy brand names even though the PDO does not allow sub-zone labelling.

appellations.name: Mantinia
appellations.summary: On a high plateau around Tripoli in Arcadia, at roughly 650 metres, Mantinia makes the most aromatic dry white in Greece from pink-skinned Moschofilero: rose petal, citrus blossom and spice, with crisp acidity and moderate alcohol. Sparkling Mantinia is permitted, and the cool, late harvest (often into October) makes this one of the latest-picked PDOs in Greece.
appellations.terroir: Cold winters, frost risk and a short season on the plateau of ancient Mantineia; clay and limestone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: Moschofilero is a 'grey' grape: skin colour ranges from pale pink to purple, and longer skin contact gives copper-tinted whites and rosés.

appellations.name: Patra
appellations.summary: The dry white appellation of Patras, made only from Roditis grown on the slopes of the Achaean mountains. Higher vineyards give citrus, minerally wines; many producers bottle Roditis as PGI instead.
appellations.terroir: Slopes from about 250 to 800 metres facing the Gulf of Patras.

appellations.name: Mavrodaphne of Patras
appellations.summary: A fortified red made since the nineteenth century around Patras, sweet and raisiny with notes of coffee, caramel and dried fig, often aged oxidatively for years in barrels. Achaia Clauss made it famous; Parparoussis and Antonopoulos have revived higher-quality versions, including old solera-style bottlings.
appellations.terroir: Coastal hills around Patras.
appellations.nerd_note: Local lore says Gustav Clauss named the wine after his late fiancée Daphne; the grape name 'black laurel' is older than that story.

appellations.name: Muscat of Patras
appellations.summary: Sweet Muscat from the hills around Patras, either fortified or made from sun-dried grapes; fragrant with orange blossom and apricot. The grape is the small-berried Muscat Blanc (Moschato Aspro), the same as on Samos, grown on the hills behind the city alongside the vineyards of PDO Patra and Mavrodaphne of Patras.
appellations.terroir: Slopes of Achaia with calcareous soils.

appellations.name: Muscat of Rio Patras
appellations.summary: A smaller Muscat appellation centred on Rio, east of Patras at the narrows of the Gulf of Corinth, for fortified or sun-dried sweet Muscat. Parparoussis makes the reference examples.
appellations.terroir: Coastal hills around Rio.

appellations.name: Monemvasia-Malvasia
appellations.summary: Registered in 2011 to revive the legendary Malmsey of the Middle Ages, this PDO covers sweet wines from sun-dried grapes made in Laconia around the rock of Monemvasia. The rules require long barrel ageing, and the best wines are amber, honeyed and nutty. Monemvasia Winery (Tsimbidis) led the revival.
appellations.terroir: Hills of south-eastern Laconia with limestone soils, hot and dry.
appellations.nerd_note: The grape called Monemvasia and the Italian Malvasia family share a name and a trade route, but DNA shows Monemvasia is a distinct Greek variety.

appellations.name: Robola of Kefalonia
appellations.summary: Kefalonia's flagship white grows on the limestone flanks of Mount Ainos, often around the Omala valley, giving lean, lemony, stony wines with a smoky edge. Many vines are ungrafted because phylloxera could not spread in the loose limestone scree. The Robola cooperative (Orealios Gaia) handles much of the crop.
appellations.terroir: Limestone scree at up to around 900 metres, very poor soils, strong sun and sea winds.
appellations.nerd_note: Robola was long assumed to be Italy's Ribolla Gialla; DNA analysis says the two are unrelated.

appellations.name: Muscat of Kefalonia
appellations.summary: Sweet Muscat from Kefalonia, fortified or from sun-dried grapes; small production, mostly sold on the island. The grape is Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, grown on the same dry limestone as Robola. Like Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia, it is a small production sold mostly on the island.

appellations.name: Mavrodaphne of Kefalonia
appellations.summary: Kefalonia's fortified red, made in the same style as Mavrodaphne of Patras. Mavrodaphne may in fact originate in the Ionian islands, and Kefalonian producers also make it dry. EU rules allow Korinthiaki (Black Corinth) alongside Mavrodaphne, as in Patras.

appellations.name: Samos
appellations.summary:
Muscat of Samos has been one of Greece's most exported wines for over a century, and it is a model of cooperative winemaking: the Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives of Samos, founded in 1934, buys grapes from thousands of growers who tend small terraces on the island's mountains. The range runs from fortified vin doux (Samos Doux, Grand Cru) to Nectar, made from sun-dried grapes and aged in oak, and long-aged Anthemis and Samos Vin Doux Naturel Grand Cru bottlings.

Altitude matters: terraces climb from near sea level to over 800 metres on Mount Ampelos and Mount Kerkis, and the higher sites ripen weeks later, giving finer, more aromatic Muscat. The same mountains are covered by PGI Plagies Ampelou, used for dry wines.
appellations.terroir: Steep, hand-built stone terraces of schist and limestone; the north-facing slopes are cooler and wetter.
producers: Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives of Samos (EOSS)
appellations.nerd_note: Samos was a tax-free supplier of Muscat to the Vatican and the Catholic church for sacramental wine in the twentieth century.

appellations.name: Limnos
appellations.summary: Limnos makes dry, floral white wine from Muscat of Alexandria, unusual in Greece, and reds from Limnio, a grape probably identical to the Lemnia vine that Aristotle described. Volcanic soils and constant wind keep yields low.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic and clay soils on a flat, windy island in the north Aegean.

appellations.name: Muscat of Limnos
appellations.summary: The sweet partner to PDO Limnos, fortified or from sun-dried grapes; grapey and floral. Unlike the Muscat Blanc of Samos and Patras, it is made from Muscat of Alexandria (Moschato Alexandreias), fortified or from sun-dried grapes, on the island's volcanic soils.

appellations.name: Paros
appellations.grapes: Mandilaria with the white Monemvasia (red); Monemvasia (white)
appellations.summary: Paros has one of the oddest rules in Europe: its red must blend the dark Mandilaria with the white Monemvasia, a historic practice that softens Mandilaria's tannin and colour. Moraitis is the main producer. Old bush vines on sand and schist are often ungrafted.
appellations.terroir: Sandy, granite and schist soils, strong winds.

appellations.name: Malvasia Paros
appellations.summary: One of the four Malvasia PDOs created in 2011: sweet wine from sun-dried Monemvasia grapes, aged in oak. Production is tiny. Its rules allow Monemvasia with a little Assyrtiko. Like the other three Malvasia PDOs of 2011, it aims to revive the sweet wine style Venetian merchants once traded from the Aegean.

appellations.name: Rhodes
appellations.summary: Rhodes' PDO covers delicate whites and sparkling wine from Athiri grown on the slopes of Mount Attavyros around Embonas, and reds from Mandilaria (locally Amorgiano). CAIR, founded under Italian rule in 1928, has made sparkling wine here for nearly a century.
appellations.terroir: Limestone slopes up to about 700 metres on the island's highest mountain.

appellations.name: Muscat of Rhodes
appellations.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Muscat Trani
appellations.summary: Sweet Muscat from Rhodes, light and floral; a small appellation, mostly cooperative. The vineyards share the slopes of the island with PDO Rhodes, and the wine is usually lighter and more floral than the Muscats of Samos or Patras. Production is small.

appellations.name: Peza
appellations.summary: South of Heraklion around the village of Peza, Crete's largest PDO makes fresh whites from Vilana and reds from Kotsifali blended with Mandilari for colour and tannin. The Peza Union of cooperatives remains important, alongside family estates such as Lyrarakis and Stilianou.
appellations.terroir: Hillsides at roughly 300 to 600 metres under the Lasithi and Psiloritis ranges; calcareous clay.

appellations.name: Archanes
appellations.summary: A red-only PDO around Archanes, a Minoan centre where the villa of Vathypetro preserves one of the oldest wine presses in Europe. Kotsifali gives perfume and alcohol, Mandilari colour and grip.
appellations.terroir: Slopes beneath Mount Giouchtas at 300 to 600 metres.
appellations.nerd_note: Vathypetro's Minoan press, a few kilometres south of Archanes, is still visible in situ.

appellations.name: Dafnes
appellations.summary: West of Heraklion, Dafnes is the home of Liatiko, an early-ripening Cretan red that gives pale, spicy dry wines and, traditionally, sweet wines from sun-dried grapes. Douloufakis is the leading estate.
appellations.terroir: Hills of 300 to 600 metres, calcareous clay.

appellations.name: Sitia
appellations.grapes: Liatiko and Mandilari (red); Vilana and Thrapsathiri (white)
appellations.summary: Eastern Crete's PDO, with some of the island's highest vineyards (up to around 600 metres or more), makes Liatiko reds, white blends and sweet Liatiko. Economou's long-aged Liatiko from the Ziros plateau is a cult bottle.
appellations.terroir: Dry, windy eastern Crete; terraces and plateaus above Sitia.

appellations.name: Malvasia Sitia
appellations.grapes: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko, Athiri
appellations.summary: A 2011 PDO for sweet wines in the medieval Cretan Malvasia tradition, made from sun-dried grapes around Sitia. Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko and Athiri are permitted. Production is still tiny, but it gives eastern Crete a sweet-wine identity alongside dry Sitia.

appellations.name: Chandakas-Candia
appellations.grapes: Vidiano, Vilana, Assyrtiko, Athiri, Thrapsathiri (white); Kotsifali, Mandilari (red)
appellations.summary: Created in 2011 around Heraklion (Chandakas was its Byzantine and Arab name, Candia its Venetian one), this PDO gives a home to modern Cretan dry wines, including Vidiano-based whites. White blends lean on Vidiano, Vilana, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko and Athiri; reds on Kotsifali and Mandilari.

appellations.name: Malvasia Chandakas-Candia
appellations.grapes: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Vidiano, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko, Athiri
appellations.summary: The Heraklion version of the Malvasia revival: sweet wines from sun-dried grapes, reviving the style Venetian Candia exported across Europe. Malvasia di Candia Aromatica leads the blend with Vidiano, Muscat Blanc, Liatiko, Thrapsathiri, Assyrtiko and Athiri permitted. Production is small; Heraklion-area producers are still building the style.

appellations.name: Commandaria
appellations.summary:
Commandaria is a sweet amber wine made from sun-dried Xynisteri and Mavro grown in 14 villages on the southern slopes of the Troodos, north of Limassol: Agios Georgios, Agios Konstantinos, Agios Mamas, Agios Pavlos, Apsiou, Gerasa, Doros, Zoopigi, Kalo Chorio, Kapilio, Laneia, Louvaras, Monagri and Silikou. Grapes are picked very ripe, laid in the sun for about a week to raise sugar to 390 to 450 grams per litre, fermented until the yeast gives up around 15 percent alcohol (fortification is allowed but not required), and aged at least two years in oak. Good Commandaria tastes of raisin, fig, carob, coffee and orange peel with enough acidity to stay fresh, and old bottlings from the solera-like 'mana' tradition can be remarkable.

The name comes from the Grande Commanderie of the Knights Templar and Hospitaller at Kolossi, which exported the wine across medieval Europe, and it is the oldest wine name in continuous use. Production fell to around 200,000 bottles a year by 2025; UNESCO's inscription of its traditions in December 2025 is meant to help revive it.
appellations.terroir: South-facing slopes of 500 to 900 metres; calcareous and volcanic soils; goblet-trained, unirrigated vines at least four years old.
appellations.nerd_note: Many old Commandaria lots were kept in a 'mana' (mother) jar, topped up with each new vintage like a solera, so a single jar could hold wine generations old.

appellations.name: Krasochoria Lemesou
appellations.grapes: Xynisteri, Maratheftiko, Mavro, Yiannoudi, Promara and international varieties
appellations.summary: The 'wine villages of Limassol' PDO covers the high villages west of the Commandaria zone, around Omodos, Vasa, Koilani, Malia and Arsos, the historic heart of Cypriot table wine. Limestone and chalk soils at 600 to 1,200 metres give fresh Xynisteri and structured Maratheftiko.

appellations.name: Krasochoria Lemesou-Afames
appellations.summary: A sub-zone of the Limassol wine villages named after the Afames hill above Pelendri and Kato Platres, on the higher, volcanic eastern side of the zone. Higher and cooler than most of the Limassol wine villages, it is planted with Xynisteri, Maratheftiko and Mavro alongside international grapes.

appellations.name: Krasochoria Lemesou-Laona
appellations.summary: A sub-zone of the Limassol wine villages around the Laona area near Arsos and Omodos, on limestone at 900 to 1,200 metres. The limestone gives fresh, saline Xynisteri, and Maratheftiko and Yiannoudi give the zone's best reds.

appellations.name: Pitsilia
appellations.grapes: Xynisteri, Maratheftiko, Mavro, Cabernet Sauvignon and others
appellations.summary: The high Pitsilia area on the eastern Troodos (around Kyperounda, Agros and Pelendri) has some of Europe's highest vineyards, up to around 1,500 metres, on igneous soils. Kyperounda's winery at about 1,450 metres is among the highest in Europe.

appellations.name: Vouni Panagias-Ambelitis
appellations.summary: A cool plateau around Panagia in the Paphos hills at 800 to 1,100 metres, the source of fresh Xynisteri and of Maratheftiko from Vouni Panagia winery. The plateau is among the coolest places to grow grapes in Cyprus, and the zone's bush vines are ungrafted, like all Cypriot vines.

appellations.name: Laona Akama
appellations.grapes: Xynisteri, Maratheftiko, Mavro, Yiannoudi and others
appellations.summary: The limestone Laona plateau above the Akamas peninsula in the north-west, around Kathikas and Kritou Terra, between 450 and 750 metres; sea breezes give some of the island's most saline whites.

appellations.name: Malta
appellations.grapes: Ġellewża, Girgentina and authorised international varieties
appellations.summary: The PDO for wine from vineyards on the main island of Malta, from terraced plots on limestone in the west and north (around Rabat, Mġarr and Siġġiewi). Delicata, Marsovin, Meridiana and Montekristo are the main producers; reds from Syrah and Merlot and whites from Chardonnay and Girgentina dominate.

appellations.name: Gozo
appellations.grapes: Ġellewża, Girgentina and authorised international varieties
appellations.summary: The PDO for the smaller island of Gozo, greener and more rural than Malta, with small family estates such as Ta' Mena and Tal-Massar around Xagħra and Għarb, near the Neolithic temples of Ġgantija.

appellations.name: Mornag
appellations.summary: The largest Tunisian appellation, on the plain and hills south-east of Tunis around Mornag, Khledia and the slopes of Djebel Ressas. Most of the country's reds and rosés come from here.

appellations.name: Grand Cru Mornag
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: The top tier of the Mornag area, from lower-yielding hillside vineyards; 'Grand Cru' is part of the registered name. It sits at the top of the Tunisian hierarchy, and its reds are often oak-aged blends that include Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon alongside the traditional Mediterranean grapes.

appellations.name: Coteaux de Tébourba
appellations.summary: Hills along the Medjerda river west of Tunis around Tébourba, once a centre of French colonial estates. The Medjerda valley's alluvial soils and hillsides give reds and rosés from Carignan and Cinsault, and a little white wine.

appellations.name: Sidi Salem
appellations.summary: A small appellation in the hinterland of Tunis; reds and rosés from Mediterranean varieties. Created in 1973 along with Mornag and Coteaux de Tébourba, it is one of the less-seen Tunisian names on export labels.

appellations.name: Coteaux d'Utique
appellations.summary: Named after the Phoenician city of Utica, older than Carthage, on the lower Medjerda north-west of Tunis. Vineyards lie on low hills near the ruins of Utica and the coast of the Gulf of Tunis, giving soft reds and rosés.

appellations.name: Kélibia
appellations.summary: Muscat de Kélibia comes from the sandy, windswept tip of Cap Bon around Kélibia, made dry and aromatic (unusually for Muscat of Alexandria) as well as sweet. Kerkouane's Punic ruins lie just north.

appellations.name: Thibar
appellations.summary: Muscat de Thibar comes from the hills of Béja governorate, where the White Fathers missionaries founded a domain in 1895 and made wine and Thibarine liqueur. It is one of Tunisia's two historic Muscat appellations, both created in 1958, alongside Kélibia.

appellations.name: Coteaux de Mascara
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Clairette
appellations.summary: The most famous Algerian name, from the hills around Mascara in the west, whose heavy, dark reds were prized for blending in colonial times and are counted among the country's best today.

appellations.name: Coteaux de Tlemcen
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Clairette
appellations.summary: Hills around the historic city of Tlemcen near the Moroccan border, at 600 to 900 metres; a source of the ONCV's Cuvée du Président blend. Higher altitude and more rain than the coastal plains give these wines more freshness than most Algerian reds.

appellations.name: Monts du Tessalah
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Clairette
appellations.summary: The Tessala mountains near Sidi Bel Abbès, south of Oran; reds and rosés. The hills sit just west of Sidi Bel Abbès in the heart of the old Oranie wine country, where colonial estates once made bulk wine for blending in southern France. Today the zone produces mainly Carignan and Cinsault reds.

appellations.name: Dahra
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Clairette
appellations.summary: The coastal Dahra massif between Mostaganem and Ténès, with sea-cooled hillside vineyards; a component of the Cuvée du Président. The Dahra hills, between the Chelif river and the sea, were one of the largest colonial wine areas.

appellations.name: Coteaux du Zaccar
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Clairette
appellations.summary: The slopes of Mount Zaccar around Miliana, south-west of Algiers. Mount Zaccar rises above the town of Miliana in the Chelif valley, and its slopes give some of the freshest reds and rosés of central Algeria. Like the other zones, it is a colonial VDQS name kept by the ONCV.

appellations.name: Médéa
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Clairette
appellations.summary: High vineyards in the Tell Atlas around Médéa, up to about 1,200 metres, among the coolest in Algeria. Altitude makes Médéa one of the coolest Algerian zones, and its reds are among the most balanced the ONCV bottles. Médéa also supplies the Cuvée du Président blend.

appellations.name: Aïn Bessem-Bouira
appellations.grapes: Carignan, Cinsault, Grenache, Alicante Bouschet, Syrah, Clairette
appellations.summary: The plateau around Aïn Bessem and Bouira, south-east of Algiers, known for rosés. The plateau lies at 500 to 700 metres between the Djurdjura and the Bibans ranges, with cool nights that suit fresh rosés and light reds from Cinsault and Grenache.

appellations.name: Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Morocco's only AOC, created in 2001 for vineyards of Celliers de Meknès on the Meknès plateau around Château Roslane, at about 600 to 700 metres in the foothills of the Middle Atlas; mainly red blends of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah aged in oak.

appellations.name: Guerrouane
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: A large AOG west of Meknès known for vin gris and soft reds; Les Celliers de Meknès and Castel source much of their wine here. Clay-limestone soils at around 500 to 600 metres and Atlantic air from the west give softer wines than the hotter east.

appellations.name: Beni M'tir
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Plateau south of Meknès at around 700 to 800 metres, among the coolest and highest Moroccan vineyards, including the area around Boufekrane and El Hajeb. The altitude and cool nights give fresher reds and some of Morocco's best whites, and Château Roslane's AOC vineyards lie at its edge.

appellations.name: Saïss
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: The Saïss plain between Meknès and Fès. The plateau lies at around 500 to 600 metres, and its clay-limestone soils supply the large Meknès wineries, mainly with reds and vin gris.

appellations.name: Zerhoune
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Hills around Moulay Idriss Zerhoun and the Roman ruins of Volubilis north of Meknès. Vines grew here in Roman times around Volubilis. Today the zone gives reds and rosés from Cinsault, Grenache, Syrah and Cabernet.

appellations.name: Berkane
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Eastern zone near the Mediterranean and the Algerian border, around Berkane; reds and rosés. The Moulouya plain and the Beni Snassen foothills have a Mediterranean climate, warmer and drier than the Meknès plateau. Wineries here make mostly reds and rosés.

appellations.name: Angad
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: The Angad plain around Oujda in the far east. One of Morocco's driest wine areas, near the Algerian border, it makes sturdy reds from Carignan, Cinsault and Grenache. It is one of the three AOGs of the Oriental region with Berkane and Beni Sadden.

appellations.name: Beni Sadden
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: A small eastern zone. It is one of the three eastern AOGs, with Berkane and Angad, in Morocco's dry Oriental region. Its exact boundaries and producers could not be verified for this atlas.

appellations.name: Gharb
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: The fertile Gharb plain around Sidi Slimane north-east of Kenitra. The fertile alluvial plain behind the Atlantic coast is better known for citrus, rice and sugar beet, and its wines are mostly everyday reds and rosés.

appellations.name: Chellah
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Named after the Roman and Merinid site of Chellah at Rabat; vineyards on the coastal hinterland. The Rabat and Casablanca hinterland was one of the main vineyard areas of the French protectorate, close to the big urban markets.

appellations.name: Zemmour
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Inland from Rabat around Khémisset. The plateau around Khémisset, between Rabat and Meknès, at 300 to 500 metres, makes reds and vin gris for the large Moroccan wineries. It is one of the five Rabat and Casablanca AOGs.

appellations.name: Zaër
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: South-east of Rabat around Rommani and Benslimane, home of Thalvin's Domaine des Ouled Thaleb. Sandy soils and Atlantic breezes give the zone fresh rosés and vin gris as well as reds.

appellations.name: Zenata
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Coastal hills between Casablanca and Mohammédia, with Atlantic influence. It makes mainly reds and rosés for the Casablanca market, and urban growth has eaten into its vineyards.

appellations.name: Sahel
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Coastal zone south of Casablanca. It is one of the five AOGs of the Rabat and Casablanca region, with Atlantic-influenced vineyards. Its exact boundaries could not be verified for this atlas.

appellations.name: Doukkala
appellations.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary: Inland from El Jadida around Boulaouane, whose Castel-owned brand was long France's best-selling imported wine. The sandy Doukkala plain is hot and flat, and most of its wine is red and rosé for the domestic and French markets.

appellations.name: Tsinandali
appellations.grapes: Rkatsiteli with at least 15% Kakhuri Mtsvane
appellations.summary: Tsinandali is the most famous dry white of Georgia and the one made in the European rather than the qvevri way: Rkatsiteli blended with Kakhuri Mtsvane, fermented clean and traditionally aged in oak before release, with notes of quince, citrus, white flowers and honey. The name belongs to the village and estate of the Chavchavadze princes on the right bank of the Alazani near Telavi, where Prince Alexander Chavchavadze ran a European-style winery in the first half of the nineteenth century, and the style is a direct descendant of his experiments. Soviet Tsinandali was the white on official tables across the USSR.
appellations.terroir: Right-bank terraces of the Alazani at 400 to 700 metres, on carbonate-rich alluvial and clay soils; cooled by night air from the Caucasus.
