appellations.nerd_note: The Tsinandali oenotheque holds more than 16,500 historic bottles; the oldest listed is a 1814 'Polish honey'.

appellations.name: Mukuzani
appellations.summary: The benchmark dry Saperavi. Mukuzani village sits on the right bank of the Alazani in the Gurjaani district, and its wines are dense, inky and high in acid, with black cherry, plum, blackberry and spice, traditionally given oak ageing before release, and capable of a decade or more. Story has it that Stalin poured Mukuzani for Churchill at Yalta. Many large companies produce it; the best come from old vines on the village's gravel terraces.
appellations.terroir: Right-bank slopes at about 400 to 700 metres; brown carbonate soils with gravel.

appellations.name: Kindzmarauli
appellations.summary: A naturally semi-sweet red from the Kvareli district on the left bank of the Alazani, beneath the Caucasus. Fermentation is stopped by chilling to keep residual sugar (typically 3 to 5 percent) without fortification, giving a soft, juicy wine of black cherry and pomegranate with Saperavi's acidity holding the sweetness in check. It has been produced commercially since 1942 and was one of the great Soviet favourites; it remains Georgia's best-known export in Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan and China.
appellations.terroir: Left-bank slopes of the Duruji river near Kvareli at 300 to 550 metres, on deep red soils with a warm microclimate.

appellations.name: Napareuli
appellations.summary: On the left bank of the Alazani north of Telavi, Napareuli makes dry Saperavi and dry Rkatsiteli. The imperial Udel estate made wine here in the nineteenth century, and today the village is a cluster of family cellars and the Twins Wine Cellar, whose qvevri museum explains the method.
appellations.terroir: Alluvial and carbonate soils near the river, 400 to 500 metres.

appellations.name: Gurjaani
appellations.summary: A dry white from around the town of Gurjaani, on the right bank in the middle Alazani. Traditionally Rkatsiteli with Mtsvane, it is often a fuller, rounder white than Tsinandali, and many producers make it in qvevri.
appellations.terroir: Terraces of the Gombori ridge foothills at 400 to 700 metres.

appellations.name: Akhasheni
appellations.summary: A naturally semi-sweet Saperavi from the village of Akhasheni in the Gurjaani district, softer and more chocolatey than Kindzmarauli. Commercial production dates from 1958. The village's right-bank slopes catch the afternoon sun, giving ripe, soft Saperavi with enough acidity to balance the sweetness.
appellations.terroir: Right-bank slopes of the Alazani at 400 to 600 metres.

appellations.name: Manavi
appellations.summary: The appellation of Kakhuri Mtsvane, around the village of Manavi in the Sagarejo district (Outer Kakheti). Its whites are aromatic and mineral, among Georgia's most elegant non-amber whites. Mtsvane from Manavi is often made both European-style and in qvevri, where it gains texture and notes of dried herbs.
appellations.terroir: Southern slopes of the Gombori range at 500 to 700 metres, drier than the Alazani valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Mtsvane means 'green', and several unrelated grapes share it; Manavi's is Mtsvane Kakhuri, the Kakhetian one.

appellations.name: Vazisubani
appellations.summary: A dry white from Vazisubani in the Gurjaani district; the name means 'vine quarter'. The Andronikashvili princes had an estate here, now a restored hotel and winery. It lies on the right bank of the Alazani between Mukuzani and Gurjaani, and its whites are made in both the European and the Kakhetian qvevri style.

appellations.name: Teliani
appellations.summary: Georgia's only appellation for an international grape: dry Cabernet Sauvignon from the Telavi area, a style made since the late nineteenth century when French varieties were planted on aristocratic estates.

appellations.name: Kardenakhi
appellations.summary: A fortified, port-like white wine from Kardenakhi in the Gurjaani district, made from very ripe Rkatsiteli, Khikhvi and Mtsvane and aged in oak. Kardenakhi village also contains the microzones of Tsarapi and Akhoebi.

appellations.name: Kotekhi
appellations.summary: A small appellation on the right bank of the middle Alazani for dry Rkatsiteli and Saperavi. Kotekhi lies just outside Gurjaani town in the middle Alazani, on the right-bank terraces. It was one of the original 18 appellations listed in 2002 and covers both a dry white and a dry red.

appellations.name: Tibaani
appellations.summary: From the Sighnaghi district in the eastern Alazani valley, Tibaani is classically a Kakhetian-method Rkatsiteli made with long skin contact, deep amber in colour and tannic: a historic appellation for what is now called orange wine.

appellations.name: Kvareli
appellations.summary: The dry red appellation of the Kvareli district on the left bank under the Caucasus, for powerful dry Saperavi. Kvareli is also home to the Khareba tunnel cellar and the Kindzmarauli Corporation.
appellations.terroir: Red and humus-calcareous soils under the mountains, 350 to 600 metres.

appellations.name: Kakheti
appellations.grapes: Rkatsiteli, Kakhuri Mtsvane, Saperavi and other permitted Kakhetian varieties
appellations.summary: The regional appellation covering all of Kakheti. Historically it meant a white wine made by the full Kakhetian method (whole-cluster maceration in qvevri); today it also covers dry whites, ambers, rosés and reds from the region, labelled Kakheti or Kakhuri. Varietal labels such as 'Kakhuri Rkatsiteli' or 'Kakhuri Mtsvane' fall under this name rather than being separate appellations.

appellations.name: Khashmis Saperavi
appellations.summary: Dry Saperavi from the village of Khashmi in Sagarejo (Outer Kakheti), on the Iori side of the Gombori ridge; the first of the new wave of microzone appellations after the original 18.

appellations.name: Akhmeta
appellations.grapes: Kakhuri Mtsvane (amber wines may include Kisi and Khikhvi)
appellations.summary: The upper Alazani around Akhmeta, cooler and closer to the Pankisi gorge, gives fresh, perfumed Mtsvane in dry, semi-dry, semi-sweet and amber styles. The zone's cooler, higher sites close to the mountains give lighter, more aromatic wines than the middle Alazani.

appellations.name: Tsarapi
appellations.grapes: Rkatsiteli with up to 15% Kakhuri Mtsvane and/or Khikhvi
appellations.summary: A microzone within Kardenakhi village in the Gurjaani district, for dry amber Rkatsiteli made with skin contact; one of the first appellations created specifically for qvevri-style amber wine. Up to 15 percent Kakhuri Mtsvane or Khikhvi may be added, but no other varieties.

appellations.name: Akhoebi
appellations.summary: A microzone near Kardenakhi for dry Saperavi, including the rare large-berried Saperavi Budeshuri. Akhoebi grapes were the source of the Soviet-era Pirosmani wine. Saperavi Budeshuri is a rare local form of Saperavi, traditionally used for softer, fruitier wines.

appellations.name: Magraani Kisi
appellations.summary: The Kisi appellation, around Magraani in the Telavi area: dry white and amber Kisi, a grape revived from near oblivion in the 2000s that gives golden, aromatic qvevri wines of pear, mango, tobacco and walnut.

appellations.name: Zegaani
appellations.summary: A microzone around the village of Zegaani in Gurjaani municipality; unusually, its rules require dry red qvevri Saperavi from organic farming. Zegaani wines are deep, tannic Saperavi built for ageing, and the microzone's rules make it one of the most demanding PDOs in Georgia.

appellations.name: Atenuri
appellations.summary: The Ateni gorge south of Gori in Shida Kartli has made crisp whites for centuries; the appellation covers fresh and traditionally sparkling wines from Chinuri and Goruli Mtsvane. The seventh-century Ateni Sioni church stands above the vines.
appellations.terroir: Cool gorge at 600 to 900 metres along the Tana river; calcareous soils.

appellations.name: Okami
appellations.grapes: Chinuri or Goruli Mtsvane (white and amber); Shavkapito (red)
appellations.summary: A small zone in Kaspi municipality, Shida Kartli, for dry white, amber and red wines from Kartli's own grapes. Chinuri and Goruli Mtsvane give crisp whites and ambers, and Shavkapito gives a light, peppery red typical of Kartli.

appellations.name: Bolnisi
appellations.grapes: Rkatsiteli, Chinuri, Goruli Mtsvane, Saperavi, Tavkveri, Shavkapito, Asuretuli Shavi
appellations.summary: Kvemo Kartli's main appellation, around the town German colonists founded in 1818 as Katharinenfeld. Bolnisi now has its own designation of origin festival and covers dry white, amber, rosé and red wines.
appellations.terroir: Volcanic and alluvial soils of the Mashavera valley at 500 to 1,000 metres.

appellations.name: Asuretuli Shala
appellations.grapes: Asuretuli Shavi with Tavkveri and Shavkapito
appellations.summary: From Asureti (the former German colony Elisabethtal) in Tetritskaro, a light, pale red traditionally made from Asuretuli Shavi; 'shala' describes its pale, rosé-like colour. Asuretuli Shavi is a local red grown almost nowhere else, and the wines are light, fresh and fruity.

appellations.name: Sviri
appellations.summary: A dry white from the Zestaponi area of Imereti, on the left bank of the Kvirila river, blending the region's three classic whites in the gentler Imeretian style. Imeretian wines here are made with only a small proportion of skins and no stems, which keeps them lighter and fresher than Kakhetian amber wines.

appellations.name: Obcha
appellations.grapes: Tsolikouri (amber, up to 15% Tsitska and/or Krakhuna); Otskhanuri Sapere (red)
appellations.summary: From Obcha in Baghdati municipality, an amber Tsolikouri and a red Otskhanuri Sapere. Registered around 2024 to 2025, it was the 30th Georgian PDO. It is one of three Imeretian PDOs, alongside Sviri and Sazanos Otskhanuri.

appellations.name: Sazanos Otskhanuri
appellations.grapes: Otskhanuri Sapere (up to 5% Saperavi from the same microzone)
appellations.summary: Dry red from the Sazano microzone at 120 to 420 metres, fermented fully on the skins in qvevri or steel. Otskhanuri Sapere is one of Georgia's most tannic grapes. It was the 33rd PDO on the National Wine Agency list.

appellations.name: Khvanchkara
appellations.summary: Georgia's most celebrated semi-sweet red comes from steep vineyards around the village of Khvanchkara near Ambrolauri in Racha. Aleksandrouli gives raspberry perfume, Mujuretuli colour and body; fermentation stops naturally in the cold autumn of the mountains, leaving sweetness, low alcohol and lively acidity. Production is tiny, fakes are common, and authentic bottles command a premium.
appellations.terroir: Limestone-rich slopes of the Rioni gorge around 450 to 750 metres; cool nights and late harvests.
appellations.nerd_note: Khvanchkara has been bottled commercially since 1907; legend says it was Stalin's favourite wine.

appellations.name: Tvishi
appellations.summary: A naturally semi-sweet (sometimes dry) white from the village of Tvishi in the Tsageri district of Lechkhumi, on the right bank of the Rioni. Late-picked Tsolikouri gives honeyed, pear-scented wine with fresh acidity.

appellations.name: Okureshis Usakhelouri
appellations.summary: A tiny microzone around Okureshi in Tsageri, Lechkhumi, for dry, semi-dry or semi-sweet red from Usakhelouri ('nameless'), a delicate, strawberry-scented grape grown on a handful of hectares. It is among the most expensive wines in Georgia.

appellations.name: Racha
appellations.grapes: Racha's local varieties (rules not verified for this atlas)
appellations.summary: A regional appellation for Racha, announced by the Georgian Ministry of Agriculture in October 2025, broadening protection beyond the single village of Khvanchkara to the upper Rioni valley around Ambrolauri.

appellations.name: Lechkhumi
appellations.grapes: Lechkhumi's local varieties (rules not verified for this atlas)
appellations.summary: A regional appellation for Lechkhumi, the Tskhenistskali valley around Tsageri, home of Usakhelouri, Orbeluri Ojaleshi and Tsolikouri; listed among Georgia's PDOs by 2025. The appellation's exact grape and style rules could not be verified for this atlas.

appellations.name: Salkhino Ojaleshi
appellations.summary: Dry red Ojaleshi from Salkhino in Martvili municipality, where the Dadiani princes of Mingrelia kept their summer residence; peppery, dark-fruited and fresh. Ojaleshi, whose name is linked to the old practice of training vines up trees, ripens late in the humid west and gives fresh, peppery wines.

appellations.name: Codru
appellations.grapes: Fetească Albă, Fetească Regală, Viorica, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Aligoté, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and others
appellations.summary: Moldova's central IGP and its biggest, covering the forested hills around Chișinău. Cool for Moldova, it is the home of the country's fresh whites and its sparkling wine industry (Cricova, Asconi, Château Vartely, Carpe Diem, Gitana), and of the underground cellars of Cricova and Mileștii Mici. Codru reds are lighter and more aromatic than those of the south.
appellations.terroir: Wooded hills of 200 to 400 metres on grey forest soils and chernozem over limestone; the forests keep humidity higher and nights cooler.
appellations.nerd_note: Wine of Moldova counted about 61,200 ha of vineyard in IGP Codru, more than half the country's wine-grape area.

appellations.name: Ștefan Vodă
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Rară Neagră, Fetească Neagră, Saperavi, Malbec, Chardonnay and others
appellations.summary: The south-eastern IGP on the lower Dniester, named after Stephen the Great, and the source of Moldova's most celebrated reds. Purcari's Negru de Purcari (Cabernet Sauvignon, Saperavi and Rară Neagră) has been made here since the nineteenth century; Et Cetera at Crocmaz and estates around Tănătari and Căușeni carry the tradition forward.
appellations.terroir: Low slopes of 100 to 200 metres within about 60 kilometres of the Black Sea; Dniester fog and sea breezes temper winter cold and summer heat on calcareous chernozem.
appellations.nerd_note: The Purcari vineyards are about 500 metres from the Dniester and less than 2 kilometres from the Ukrainian border.

appellations.name: Valul lui Traian
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Fetească Neagră, Saperavi, Pinot Noir, Muscat, Chardonnay and others
appellations.summary: The southern IGP, named after the Roman-era earthworks known as Trajan's Wall, is the warmest and driest part of Moldova. Reds make up about 60 percent of its plantings and ripen fully; it also keeps the dessert-wine traditions of Ciumai and Tomai. Large wineries in Gagauzia and around Cahul make much of the volume.
appellations.terroir: Rolling plateaus of 100 to 250 metres, chernozem on loess, hot summers with drought risk.
appellations.nerd_note: About 43,200 ha of vineyard lie in this IGP.

appellations.name: Divin
appellations.summary: A geographical indication for Moldovan wine brandy, covering the whole country. Divin must be double-distilled from wine and aged at least three years in oak; it replaced the Soviet-era name 'cognac'. Leading houses include Kvint (Tiraspol), Călărași Divin and Barza Albă.
appellations.nerd_note: Divin covers the whole territory, including Transnistria, where the Kvint distillery has made brandy since 1897.

appellations.name: Ciumai
appellations.summary: A historic appellation from the village of Ciumai in the Taraclia district, known for a deep red dessert wine in the 'Cahor' style once supplied to the Russian Orthodox church. The name was one of Moldova's first designations of origin protected in the EU.

appellations.name: Romănești
appellations.summary: The historic estate and village of Romănești in the Strășeni district, Codru, whose Bordeaux-style reds were made for the imperial and later Soviet elite. Romănești was among Moldova's first designations of origin protected in the EU.

sites.name: Akrotiri (Bronze Age Thera)
sites.text: The Minoan-era town buried by the eruption of Thera around 1600 BC, preserved with storage jars, pithoi and drinking vessels under metres of pumice. The same eruption laid down the ash in which Santorini's ungrafted Assyrtiko now grows, which makes this the rare archaeological site where the ancient catastrophe is also the modern terroir.

sites.name: Vathypetro Minoan wine press
sites.text: A Minoan villa south of Archanes, built around 1600 BC, with a stone wine press, a spouted basin and storage jars still in place. It is one of the oldest wine-making installations in Europe and sits inside today's PDO Archanes.

sites.name: Dikili Tash
sites.text: A Neolithic tell near Philippi in eastern Macedonia where charred grape pips and pressed grape skins from around 4300 BC point to early wine making, perhaps the oldest such evidence in the Aegean.

sites.name: Palace of Nestor, Pylos
sites.text: Mycenaean palace of the thirteenth century BC whose Linear B archive records wine and vineyards and whose wine magazine held dozens of storage jars, some sealed with clay stamped with the wine ideogram.

sites.name: Ancient Thasos (Limenas)
sites.text: The harbour city of Thasos, whose fifth-century BC inscriptions regulated the sale of wine and whose stamped amphorae spread its famous sweet wine across the Aegean and Black Sea.

sites.name: Ariousian hills of Chios
sites.text: The north-west of Chios, around Volissos, produced Ariousian wine, the most prized wine of classical Greece, shipped in amphorae stamped with a sphinx. Vines barely survive there today.

sites.name: Temple of Zeus, Ancient Nemea
sites.text: The fourth-century BC temple of the Nemean Games stands among Agiorgitiko vineyards; the site museum displays wine vessels and the stadium sits a short walk away.

sites.name: Monemvasia
sites.text: The fortified rock-town whose port gave its name to Malvasia and Malmsey, the sweet wine Venetian galleys carried to Europe. PDO Monemvasia-Malvasia (2011) revives the style in the hills inland.

sites.name: Domaine Sigalas
sites.text: Paris Sigalas, a mathematician, founded his winery in 1991 on the flat Baxedes plain below Oia, in Santorini's north. Its Assyrtikos, single-site Kavalieros, Nykteri and Vinsanto are among the island's references, and the estate has bottled rare Mavrotragano reds.

sites.name: Hatzidakis Winery
sites.text: Founded by Haridimos Hatzidakis in 1997 near Pyrgos and run by his family since his death in 2017, Hatzidakis makes some of Santorini's most intense, low-intervention Assyrtikos from old vines, including the single-site Mylos and Skitali bottlings.

sites.name: Gaia Wines Santorini
sites.text: Gaia's island winery occupies an old tomato-processing plant on the beach near Exo Gonia; Thalassitis ('from the sea') was one of the first Santorini wines to win international attention, and the winery experiments with ageing wine under the sea.

sites.name: Estate Argyros
sites.text: A family estate at Episkopi Gonias founded in 1903, with some of the largest holdings of old Assyrtiko on the island and a library of Vinsanto aged for decades.

sites.name: Santo Wines
sites.text: The Union of Santorini Cooperatives, founded in 1947, with a cliff-top winery near Pyrgos above the caldera. It processes much of the island's crop.

sites.name: Kir-Yianni
sites.text: Yiannis Boutaris founded Kir-Yianni in 1997 on the family's Yiannakochori vineyard east of Naoussa, aiming for site-specific Xinomavro (Ramnista, Diaporos) and later adding the Samaropetra estate in Amyndeon.

sites.name: Thymiopoulos Vineyards
sites.text: Apostolos Thymiopoulos farms biodynamically at Trilofo and Fytia in the southern part of Naoussa, making perfumed, transparent Xinomavro such as 'Earth and Sky' and the single-vineyard Ramnista.

sites.name: Boutari Naoussa winery
sites.text: Boutari was founded in Naoussa in 1879 and its Naoussa red was for decades the bottle that defined Xinomavro abroad; its Naoussa winery is at Stenimachos, east of the town.

sites.name: Ktima Gerovassiliou
sites.text: Evangelos Gerovassiliou's estate at Epanomi, south of Thessaloniki, planted from 1981 on sandy soils by the sea. It made Malagousia famous and houses a museum of corkscrews and wine tools.

sites.name: Domaine Porto Carras
sites.text: The estate John Carras built on the slopes of Mount Meliton from the 1960s with Émile Peynaud's advice, one of the first modern wineries in Greece and the sole producer of PDO Slopes of Meliton.

sites.name: Alpha Estate
sites.text: Founded in 1997 by Angelos Iatridis and Makis Mavridis on the Amyndeon plateau, Alpha is known for its ungrafted 'Hedgehog' Xinomavro and its Malagousia and Syrah blends.

sites.name: Domaine Skouras
sites.text: George Skouras, trained in Dijon, built his winery at Malandreni near Argos; Megas Oenos (Agiorgitiko and Cabernet) was a landmark Greek blend, and his Nemea wines come from high vineyards around Gymno.

sites.name: Gaia Estate Nemea
sites.text: Gaia's Nemea winery at Koutsi, in the middle altitude band many consider Nemea's best, makes Gaia Estate Agiorgitiko, one of the benchmarks for ageable Nemea.

sites.name: Domaine Tselepos
sites.text: Yiannis Tselepos, trained in Burgundy, founded his winery at Rizes near Tegea on the Mantinia plateau in 1989; his Moschofilero, sparkling Amalia and Avlotopi Cabernet are classics.

sites.name: Achaia Clauss
sites.text: The castle-like winery Gustav Clauss founded in 1861 in the hills above Patras, home of the most famous Mavrodaphne and of cellars holding barrels and bottles back to the nineteenth century.

sites.name: Samos Wine Museum (EOSS)
sites.text: The cooperative union's old winery at Malagari near Vathy has been turned into a museum of Samian Muscat, with giant barrels and old presses; the working winery is at Karlovasi.
producers: Union of Vinicultural Cooperatives of Samos

sites.name: Orealios Gaia Robola Cooperative
sites.text: The Robola producers' cooperative in the Omala valley on Kefalonia, beneath the limestone flanks of Mount Ainos, produces a large share of PDO Robola.

sites.name: Monemvasia Winery (Tsimbidis)
sites.text: George Tsimbidis led the revival of Monemvasia-Malvasia, the first modern sweet wine in the medieval style, from vineyards at Velies in Laconia.

sites.name: Emery Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1923 at Embonas beneath Mount Attavyros, Emery makes Athiri whites and sparkling wines from some of the highest vineyards on Rhodes.

sites.name: Lyrarakis Winery
sites.text: The Lyrarakis family at Alagni, south of Heraklion, rescued the Cretan whites Dafni and Plyto from near extinction in the 1990s and is one of the leading names in Peza and Archanes.

sites.name: Douloufakis Winery
sites.text: A family winery in the village of Dafnes, west of Heraklion, run by Nikos Douloufakis, making benchmark Liatiko in dry and sun-dried sweet styles alongside Vidiano. Dafnes is the PDO built around Liatiko, an early-ripening Cretan red that gives pale, spicy, surprisingly fresh wines.

sites.name: Economou Winery, Ziros
sites.text: Yiannis Economou, who trained in Piedmont and Bordeaux, makes long-aged Liatiko from the Ziros plateau in eastern Crete, released after many years in cellar.

sites.name: Tsantali Rapsani
sites.text: Tsantali revived the Rapsani appellation from 1991, terracing the Olympus foothills and restoring the Xinomavro, Krassato and Stavroto field blend.

sites.name: Zafeirakis Winery
sites.text: The Zafeirakis family at Tyrnavos in Thessaly revived Limniona, a nearly lost ancient red, and made it a symbol of Greek variety rediscovery.

sites.name: Glinavos Winery, Zitsa
sites.text: A family winery in Zitsa, in the mountains north of Ioannina, and the reference producer for the PDO's still and semi-sparkling Debina. The high, wet Epirus climate keeps the grapes late-ripening and fresh, with low alcohol.

sites.name: Mesogeia retsina vineyards
sites.text: The plain east of Athens around Spata, Markopoulo and Koropi, historic home of Savatiano bush vines and retsina, now squeezed by suburbs and the airport.

sites.name: Kolossi Castle
sites.text: The keep of the Grande Commanderie of the Knights Hospitaller, rebuilt in 1454 on an earlier crusader castle west of Limassol. From here the knights ran the estates whose sweet wine took the name Commandaria; a medieval sugar mill stands beside it.

sites.name: Cyprus Wine Museum, Erimi
sites.text: A museum in the village of Erimi, where Chalcolithic flasks with wine residues of about 3500 BC were found, telling the story of 5,500 years of Cypriot wine.

sites.name: Pyrgos-Mavroraki
sites.text: Bronze Age industrial site of about 2000 BC in the Limassol hills, with a perfumery, olive press and winery that yielded grape seeds and wine jars.

sites.name: Omodos
sites.text: The best-known of the Limassol wine villages, around the Timios Stavros monastery, with an old communal wine press (linos) and many small wineries.

sites.name: Kyperounda Winery
sites.text: One of the highest wineries in Europe, at around 1,450 metres in Pitsilia; makes Xynisteri, Petritis and Commandaria.

sites.name: Zoopigi
sites.text: One of the 14 villages entitled to make Commandaria under the 1990 law, high in the hills north of Limassol. Growers here leave Xynisteri and Mavro to over-ripen on goblet-trained, unirrigated vines, then dry the bunches in the sun before pressing.

sites.name: Kalo Chorio (Limassol)
sites.text: Commandaria village in the hills north of Limassol and one of the centres of the traditional sweet-wine trade. Grapes are laid out on roofs and terraces for about a week to concentrate their sugar before pressing, the method Hesiod described almost three thousand years ago.

sites.name: Doros
sites.text: One of the 14 Commandaria villages, on the slopes of the Kouris valley at around 500 to 800 metres. Small producers here keep the tradition of fermenting sun-dried Mavro and Xynisteri until the yeast stops naturally at about 15 percent alcohol.

sites.name: Laneia
sites.text: A stone-built Commandaria village above the Kouris river, with a restored traditional wine press and old cellar houses. Its terraces of bush-trained Mavro and Xynisteri are part of the zone protected by the 1990 Commandaria law.

sites.name: Monagri
sites.text: Commandaria village on the slopes of the Kouris valley, known for its Byzantine monastery of Panagia Amasgou. The south-facing terraces catch full sun, ideal for drying grapes.

sites.name: Kathikas
sites.text: Village on the limestone Laona plateau above the Akamas peninsula, at the centre of the Laona Akama PDO. Several small wineries here make saline Xynisteri and Maratheftiko from vineyards at around 600 metres that catch the sea breeze.

sites.name: Koilani
sites.text: One of the Limassol wine villages on the southern Troodos, with old stone wine presses and a small church museum. Its high vineyards supply the Krasochoria Lemesou PDO, mostly Xynisteri and Mavro on limestone and chalk.

sites.name: Marsovin Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1919 by the Cassar family at Paola; makes the traditional-method sparkling Cassar de Malte and estate wines from its own vineyards.

sites.name: Emmanuel Delicata Winery
sites.text: Malta's oldest wine company, founded in 1907, on the harbour at Paola; works with contracted growers across both islands.

sites.name: Ta' Mena Estate
sites.text: A family farm and winery near Xagħra on Gozo making DOK Gozo wines alongside olive oil and cheese.

sites.name: Meridiana Wine Estate
sites.text: Founded in 1987 at Ta' Qali, near Mdina, with advice from Antinori; one of the first estates to bottle Maltese-grown international varieties.

sites.name: Kavaklıdere winery
sites.text: Founded in Ankara in 1929 and now based at Akyurt north-east of the capital, Kavaklıdere is Türkiye's largest private wine producer, with vineyards in Cappadocia, the Aegean and Thrace; its Pendore and Çankaya brands are national classics.

sites.name: Vinkara, Kalecik
sites.text: A winery in Kalecik on the Kızılırmak, near the village that gave its name to Kalecik Karası; known for still and traditional-method sparkling Kalecik Karası.

sites.name: Turasan winery, Ürgüp
sites.text: A Cappadocian family winery founded in 1943 in Ürgüp with cellars cut into the tuff; makes Emir, Narince and Öküzgözü.

sites.name: Kocabağ, Uçhisar
sites.text: Family winery at Uçhisar in Cappadocia, beside the fairy chimneys of Göreme, specialising in Emir and local reds.

sites.name: Urla Şarapçılık
sites.text: Can Ortabaş's winery on the Urla peninsula west of İzmir, which led the revival of the near-extinct Urla Karası and of Aegean vineyards abandoned after 1923.

sites.name: Corvus Vineyards, Bozcaada
sites.text: Architect Reşit Soley's estate on Bozcaada (ancient Tenedos), working the island's Karalahna and Çavuş alongside international grapes.

sites.name: Doluca, Mürefte
sites.text: Founded in 1926 by Nihat Kutman at Mürefte on the Sea of Marmara, once a Greek wine village; Doluca introduced many international varieties to Türkiye.

sites.name: Chamlija
sites.text: Mustafa Çamlıca's estate in Büyükkarıştıran, Kırklareli, one of the leading boutique wineries of Thrace, known for Papazkarası and blends.

sites.name: Hattusa
sites.text: The Hittite capital, whose archives include laws protecting vineyards and texts on wine offerings; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sites.name: Kültepe (Kanesh)
sites.text: The Bronze Age city and Assyrian merchant colony near Kayseri whose tablets record trade in wine around 1900 BC.

sites.name: Château Musar
sites.text: Gaston Hochar's winery, founded in 1930 in an eighteenth-century castle at Ghazir above Jounieh Bay. Grapes travel from Bekaa vineyards over the mountains; the red (Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault, Carignan) is released after about seven years and the white is old-vine Obaideh and Merwah. Serge Hochar's 'natural' approach and its long-lived, variable vintages made it a cult wine.

sites.name: Château Ksara
sites.text: Lebanon's oldest and largest winery, founded by Jesuit priests in 1857 near Zahlé. In 1898 the Jesuits found Roman-era caves, now about two kilometres of cellars at constant temperature; the Vatican told the order to sell in 1972, and a Lebanese consortium bought it. About 3 million bottles a year.

sites.name: Château Kefraya
sites.text: An estate in the West Bekaa on the slopes of Mount Barouk, founded as a winery in 1979 by Michel de Bustros; its Comte de M is one of Lebanon's top reds. During the 1982 invasion its French winemaker was arrested as a spy until he proved he made wine.

sites.name: Massaya
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by the brothers Sami and Ramzi Ghosn with partners from Bordeaux and the Rhône (including Vieux Télégraphe's Brunier family), at Tanail in the central Bekaa; famous for its terrace restaurant and Cinsault-based reds.

sites.name: Temple of Bacchus, Baalbek
sites.text: One of the best-preserved Roman temples in the world, built in the second century AD in the sanctuary of Heliopolis at Baalbek; its portal is carved with vines, grape clusters and Bacchic scenes. A UNESCO World Heritage Site at the northern end of the Bekaa wine zone.

sites.name: Byblos
sites.text: One of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world, whose wine was shipped to Old Kingdom Egypt.

sites.name: Tell el-Burak Phoenician wine press
sites.text: A seventh-century BC plastered wine press, one of the largest known in the Phoenician world, excavated south of Sidon with traces of nearby vineyards.

sites.name: Château Marsyas
sites.text: The Saadé family's estate in the West Bekaa near Kefraya, making structured Cabernet and Syrah blends.

sites.name: Tel Kabri palace wine cellar
sites.text: The Canaanite palace on the grounds of Kibbutz Kabri, near Nahariya, where in 2013 archaeologists found a storeroom of about 40 large jars, around 2,000 litres, with residues of red wine flavoured with resins, honey and herbs, dated to about 1700 BC. The palace also had Minoan-style frescoes and was destroyed by an earthquake.

sites.name: Carmel Winery, Zichron Ya'akov
sites.text: The cellars Baron Edmond de Rothschild built in 1892 for the colony of Zichron Ya'akov on Mount Carmel's southern slopes, still Carmel's winery and visitor centre.

sites.name: Carmel Winery, Rishon LeZion
sites.text: Rothschild's first great winery, completed in 1890 at Rishon LeZion, with historic underground cellars; long the heart of Israel's sacramental wine trade.

sites.name: Golan Heights Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1983 at Katzrin by Golan settlements, the winery behind the Yarden, Gamla and Golan labels and the first to prove the high Golan's potential for Cabernet and sparkling wine. The Golan is Syrian territory occupied by Israel since 1967.

sites.name: Domaine du Castel
sites.text: Eli Ben Zaken's family estate in the Judean Hills, founded in 1988 at Ramat Raziel, with its winery now at Yad HaShmona; its Grand Vin was among the first Israeli wines praised internationally.

sites.name: Shivta Byzantine wine presses
sites.text: A Byzantine town in the Negev (UNESCO Incense Route) with large wine presses and evidence that it made and exported wine in the sixth and seventh centuries.

sites.name: Avdat
sites.text: Nabataean and Byzantine city on the Incense Route in the Negev, with ancient wine presses on its hillsides.

sites.name: Dalton Winery
sites.text: In the Dalton industrial park of the Upper Galilee, part of a cluster of seven wineries including Recanati and Adir.

sites.name: Flam Winery
sites.text: The Flam family's winery in the Judean Hills near Eshtaol, one of Israel's leading boutique producers.

sites.name: Tabor Winery
sites.text: Winery at Kfar Tavor beneath Mount Tabor in the Lower Galilee, on chalk and terra rossa.

sites.name: Cremisan Monastery winery
sites.text: The Salesian monastery on a terraced hillside between Beit Jala and Jerusalem has made wine since 1885 and now bottles the ancient Palestinian grapes Hamdani, Jandali, Dabouki and Baladi bought from Hebron-area growers.

sites.name: Taybeh Winery
sites.text: The Khoury family's winery, opened in 2013 next to their brewery in the Christian village of Taybeh, north-east of Ramallah.

sites.name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra)
sites.text: The Bronze Age port city near Latakia whose archives record vineyards and wine exports, and which gave the world one of its first alphabets.

sites.name: Mari (Tell Hariri)
sites.text: Palace of the kings of Mari on the Euphrates whose eighteenth-century BC tablets record wine shipments and royal preferences.

sites.name: Domaine de Bargylus
sites.text: The Saadé family's vineyard on the Jebel Ansariyeh east of Latakia, at about 900 metres, Syria's only internationally distributed wine estate; it kept producing through the civil war.

sites.name: Little Petra (Siq al-Barid)
sites.text: A Nabataean suburb north of Petra with rock-cut wine presses, cisterns and banquet halls, evidence of winemaking in the desert two thousand years ago.

sites.name: Umm Qais (Gadara)
sites.text: The Decapolis city of Gadara, above the Sea of Galilee and the Yarmouk, renowned in Roman times for its wine.

sites.name: Abydos, tomb U-j
sites.text: In the royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa'ab at Abydos, the tomb of a ruler of about 3150 BC (often called Scorpion I) contained dozens of imported wine jars with residues of resin and herbs, plus grape seeds and skins, and ivory labels that are among the earliest Egyptian writing.

sites.name: Tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62)
sites.text: The king's tomb in the Valley of the Kings held more than two dozen wine jars, most with ink dockets naming the regnal year, the estate (often in the western Delta), the chief vintner and the colour; analysis identified red, white and shedeh.

sites.name: Tomb of Nakht, Sheikh Abd el-Qurna
sites.text: Theban tomb TT52, about 1400 BC, whose painted vintage scene shows grape picking from a pergola, treading in a vat and the filling of amphorae.

sites.name: Gianaclis (Alexandria)
sites.text: Alexandria home of the Gianaclis brand, founded by Nestor Gianaclis, who planted Egypt's first modern vineyard south of the city in 1882; now part of Al Ahram Beverages (Heineken). The vineyards themselves lie in the desert south of Alexandria.

sites.name: Lake Mareotis
sites.text: The lake south of Alexandria whose shores produced Mareotic wine, praised by Horace and Virgil, in Ptolemaic and Roman times.

sites.name: Kharga Oasis
sites.text: Western Desert oasis whose Roman-era fortresses and settlements had vineyards and wine presses; oasis wine was famous in late antiquity.

sites.name: Beni Hasan
sites.text: Middle Kingdom rock tombs whose paintings show grape harvesting and treading; Kouroum of the Nile's vineyards lie nearby on the Nile.

sites.name: Carthage
sites.text: The Phoenician and Punic metropolis whose agronomist Mago wrote the classic treatise on farming and viticulture; destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and rebuilt as a Roman city. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sites.name: Kerkouane
sites.text: The best-preserved Punic town, on Cap Bon near Kélibia, abandoned in the third century BC and never rebuilt (UNESCO).

sites.name: Domaine Neferis
sites.text: A Tunisian-Italian estate near Grombalia on Cap Bon, one of the modern wineries built since the late 1990s.

sites.name: Domaine Atlas
sites.text: A Tunisian-German estate near Bou Argoub on Cap Bon, one of the private wineries founded after the sector opened to foreign investment in the late 1990s. It makes AOC and Premier Cru reds and rosés from Mediterranean grapes on sandy coastal soils.

sites.name: Kélibia
sites.text: Fishing town at the tip of Cap Bon and centre of AOC Muscat de Kélibia.

sites.name: Thibar
sites.text: Village in the Béja hills where the White Fathers planted vines in the 1890s; home of Muscat de Thibar.

sites.name: Mornag
sites.text: Town on the plain south-east of Tunis at the heart of Tunisia's largest appellation, created in 1973. French colonists planted the area after 1881; today its reds and rosés from Carignan, Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah supply much of the country's wine.

sites.name: Mascara
sites.text: Hill town south-east of Oran, centre of the Coteaux de Mascara zone and of colonial Algeria's most famous wines.

sites.name: Médéa
sites.text: Highland town in the Tell Atlas south of Algiers, centre of the Médéa zone with vineyards up to about 1,200 metres.

sites.name: Tlemcen
sites.text: Historic city of Zayyanid mosques near the Moroccan border at the heart of the Coteaux de Tlemcen, one of Algeria's seven quality zones. Vineyards on the surrounding hills at 600 to 900 metres supply the ONCV's Cuvée du Président blend.

sites.name: Sidi Brahim
sites.text: Village near Sidi Bel Abbès whose name became one of the best-known Algerian wine brands in France.

sites.name: Château Roslane
sites.text: The Celliers de Meknès flagship estate in the foothills of the Middle Atlas near El Hajeb, granted Morocco's first château status in 2009; its vineyards make AOC Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru.

sites.name: Volubilis
sites.text: Roman city near Meknès (UNESCO) with olive presses and Bacchic mosaics, at the centre of today's Zerhoune and Guerrouane wine zones.

sites.name: Domaine des Ouled Thaleb (Thalvin)
sites.text: One of Morocco's oldest wineries, founded in the 1920s near Benslimane in the Zaër zone, run by Thalvin.

sites.name: Boulaouane
sites.text: Kasbah village in the Doukkala whose name became the brand of Morocco's most exported wine.

sites.name: Meknès
sites.text: Imperial city of the Alaouite sultan Moulay Ismail and the capital of Moroccan wine, seat of Celliers de Meknès, the company Brahim Zniber built into the producer of about 85 percent of the country's wine by 2016. Most AOG zones of the Saïss plateau surround it.

sites.name: Cyrene
sites.text: Greek city founded around 630 BC by settlers from Thera, in the wet Jebel Akhdar, where vines and olives grew; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sites.name: Gadachrili Gora
sites.text: A low Neolithic mound near the village of Imiri, south of Marneuli, cut through by the Shulaveri stream. Jars from its round mudbrick houses, dated to about 6000 to 5800 BC, held the oldest chemical traces of grape wine yet found (tartaric, malic, succinic and citric acids), and one contained grape pollen. A museum is planned on the site.

sites.name: Shulaveris Gora
sites.text: The type site of the Shulaveri-Shomu culture, a few kilometres from Gadachrili Gora, which yielded the second set of Neolithic wine jars published in 2017, along with some of the earliest bread wheat in the Caucasus.

sites.name: Alaverdi Monastery cellar
sites.text: The eleventh-century cathedral of Alaverdi rises above the Alazani valley; its monastic wine cellar, restored in 2006 with the support of Badagoni, holds more than 40 qvevri, and the monks' qvevri wines are among Georgia's most respected. The monastery hosts the Alaverdoba harvest festival in September.

sites.name: Tsinandali Estate (Chavchavadze)
sites.text: The country house of Prince Alexander Chavchavadze, poet, general and Georgia's first great modern winemaker, with its Italianate palace, English garden and a cellar of more than 16,500 historic bottles from 1814 onwards. Raided by Imam Shamil's forces in 1854, later owned by the Russian imperial family, it is now a museum, hotel and home of the Tsinandali classical music festival.

sites.name: Gremi citadel
sites.text: The hilltop citadel and Church of the Archangels of Gremi, capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti from the fifteenth century until Shah Abbas I destroyed it in 1615 to 1616, an invasion that emptied Kakheti's vineyards for generations.

sites.name: Ikalto Academy
sites.text: Monastery founded by St Zenon in the sixth century and an academy in the twelfth, where viticulture and winemaking were reportedly taught; a huge stone wine press and qvevri remain in the grounds. Tradition says Shota Rustaveli studied here.

sites.name: Nekresi Monastery
sites.text: One of the oldest Christian sites in Kakheti, on a forested slope above the Alazani valley, with old qvevri cellars and a fourth-century basilica.

sites.name: Khareba wine tunnel
sites.text: A 7.7-kilometre tunnel carved into the rock near Kvareli in the 1950s as a military facility and now used by the Khareba winery as a cellar, holding a steady 12 to 14 degrees C.

sites.name: Pheasant's Tears
sites.text: Founded in 2007 in hilltop Sighnaghi by the American painter John Wurdeman and the Georgian grower Gela Patalishvili; its long-macerated qvevri Rkatsiteli, Kisi and Saperavi helped introduce the world to Georgian natural wine.

sites.name: Okro's Wines
sites.text: Okro Natroshvili's small natural-wine cellar in Sighnaghi, making qvevri wines from Rkatsiteli, Mtsvane, Saperavi and rare Kakhetian grapes.

sites.name: Iago's Wine, Chardakhi
sites.text: Iago Bitarishvili makes amber and skin-free Chinuri in qvevri in the village of Chardakhi in the Mukhrani valley of Kartli, one of the first certified organic wineries in Georgia.

sites.name: Château Mukhrani
sites.text: The estate Prince Ivane Mukhranbatoni founded in the 1870s, exporting wine to Europe in the nineteenth century; restored and replanted in the 2000s on the Mukhrani plain north-west of Tbilisi.

sites.name: Twins Wine Cellar
sites.text: The Kapanadze twins' winery in Napareuli includes a qvevri museum explaining how the vessels are made, lined with beeswax and buried.

sites.name: Ateni Sioni Church
sites.text: Seventh-century church in the Ateni gorge south of Gori, standing among the vineyards of PDO Atenuri.

sites.name: Sioni Cathedral, Tbilisi
sites.text: Tbilisi's Sioni Cathedral keeps the Grapevine Cross attributed to St Nino, the symbol of Georgian Christianity and wine.

sites.name: Khvanchkara village
sites.text: The Racha village above the Rioni gorge whose steep slopes give the famous semi-sweet Khvanchkara from Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli.

sites.name: Vardzia cave monastery
sites.text: The twelfth-century cave city of Queen Tamar carved into a cliff of the upper Mtkvari, with wine cellars and buried qvevri; the terraces around it were once vineyards and are being replanted.

sites.name: Mukuzani village
sites.text: The right-bank village in Gurjaani municipality whose gravel and carbonate terraces above the Alazani give Georgia's benchmark dry Saperavi. Mukuzani was one of the first 18 appellations listed in 2002 and is traditionally oak-aged before release.

sites.name: Kindzmarauli Corporation, Kvareli
sites.text: A large Kvareli winery and one of the main producers of semi-sweet Kindzmarauli and of Khvanchkara.

sites.name: Shumi Winery and vine collection
sites.text: A Tsinandali winery with a wine museum and a large collection vineyard of Georgian and foreign grape varieties beside the road from Telavi.

sites.name: Okureshi
sites.text: Hillside village in Tsageri, Lechkhumi, home of the rare Usakhelouri grape; its few hectares supply PDO Okureshis Usakhelouri.

sites.name: Tvishi
sites.text: Lechkhumi village on the right bank of the Rioni that gives its name to semi-sweet Tsolikouri.

sites.name: Zegaani
sites.text: Village in Gurjaani municipality whose microzone has had its own PDO since 2022, unusual in requiring dry red Saperavi made in qvevri from organically farmed grapes. It lies on the right bank of the Alazani between Mukuzani and Akhasheni.

sites.name: Magraani
sites.text: Village in the upper Alazani valley in Akhmeta municipality, at the heart of PDO Magraani Kisi (2021). Kisi, revived since the 2000s, gives golden, aromatic qvevri wines here, cooled by air off the Caucasus.

sites.name: Kardenakhi
sites.text: Gurjaani-district village of fortified Kardenakhi and the microzones Tsarapi and Akhoebi; the Andronikashvili princes had an estate here.

sites.name: Salkhino palace of the Dadiani
sites.text: The Dadiani princes' summer residence near Martvili, whose name lives on in PDO Salkhino Ojaleshi.

sites.name: Vani archaeological site
sites.text: The ancient Colchian city of Vani in Imereti (8th to 1st century BC), rich in gold work and in imported Greek amphorae that show Colchis trading wine with the Greek world.

sites.name: Tibaani
sites.text: Village in the Sighnaghi district, in the eastern Alazani valley, whose appellation is a historic name for long-macerated amber Rkatsiteli.

sites.name: Areni-1 cave winery
sites.text: A three-chambered karst cave above the Arpa river where a winery of about 4100 to 4000 BC was excavated from 2007: a clay basin for treading grapes, a 60-centimetre vat, storage jars, cups and domesticated grape remains, with malvidin residues confirmed in 2011. The cave also yielded the world's oldest leather shoe (about 3500 BC).

sites.name: Teishebaini (Karmir Blur)
sites.text: Urartian fortress of King Rusa II, built in the seventh century BC on the Red Hill at the edge of Yerevan and burnt around 585 BC. Its storerooms were lined with rows of karases, giant clay jars sunk into the floor and marked with their capacity; excavations from 1939 to 1971 recovered hundreds of them.

sites.name: Erebuni Fortress
sites.text: The fortress founded by the Urartian king Argishti I in 782 BC, origin of Yerevan; its storerooms included wine jars, and a museum displays karases.

sites.name: Noravank Monastery
sites.text: Thirteenth-century monastery in a red-rock gorge near Areni, with carved grapevines on its churches, at the heart of Vayots Dzor wine country.

sites.name: Zorah Wines, Rind
sites.text: Founded by Zorik Gharibian, an Armenian-Italian fashion entrepreneur, with vineyards of ungrafted Areni at about 1,400 metres in Rind; its Karasì red, aged in karases, helped put Armenian wine on the world map.

sites.name: Trinity Canyon Vineyards
sites.text: A pioneering estate at Aghavnadzor in Vayots Dzor, making Areni, Voskehat and karas-aged wines at about 1,400 metres.

sites.name: Voskevaz Winery
sites.text: Historic winery in Voskevaz on Aragats' southern slopes, founded in 1932, which revived karas winemaking.

sites.name: ArmAs
sites.text: Estate at Nor Yedesia in Aragatsotn with one of Armenia's largest modern vineyards and a winery making native and international varieties.

sites.name: Yerevan Brandy Company (Ararat)
sites.text: The brandy house founded in 1887 and bought by Nikolay Shustov's company in 1899, maker of Ararat brandy; owned by Pernod Ricard since 1998. Its cellars by the Hrazdan river hold barrels laid down for famous visitors.

sites.name: Göygöl wine plant (Helenendorf)
sites.text: Göygöl, founded as Helenendorf in 1819 by Swabian colonists, kept its German houses, Lutheran church and the wine and cognac plant founded in 1860, today run by Vinagro.

sites.name: Madrasa village
sites.text: Village near Shamakhi that gave its name to the Madrasa (Matrassa) grape, the signature red of eastern Azerbaijan.

sites.name: Savalan (Aspi Winery)
sites.text: Aspi Winery's estate at Savalan in the Qabala district, at the foot of the Greater Caucasus, established in the late 2000s; its Savalan wines are Azerbaijan's best-known exports.

sites.name: Chabiant
sites.text: Winery in Ismayilli district at the foot of the Greater Caucasus, making Madrasa and international varieties.

sites.name: Cricova underground wine city
sites.text: Cricova's limestone galleries were dug from the fifteenth century to quarry building stone for Chișinău and converted into a wine city in the 1950s: about 120 kilometres of tunnels, half used for wine, with 'streets' named after the wines stored in them (Cabernet Street, Feteasca Street), held at about 12 degrees C all year. It is Moldova's traditional-method sparkling house and keeps the national collection, about 1.3 million bottles including wines from Hermann Göring's cellar, seized by the Soviets in 1945. Yuri Gagarin is said to have visited in 1966 and emerged two days later; Vladimir Putin celebrated his 50th birthday here.

sites.name: Mileștii Mici
sites.text: A state wine complex founded in 1969 in former limestone mines about 18 kilometres south of Chișinău. The galleries run for about 200 kilometres, of which 55 are used, at 12 to 14 degrees C and 85 to 95 percent humidity. In August 2005 Guinness World Records listed its collection, about 1.5 million bottles at the time, as the largest wine collection in the world; visitors drive through the tunnels.

sites.name: Purcari Winery
sites.text: Established in 1827 by a decree of Tsar Nicholas I as Bessarabia's first specialised winery, on a slope 500 metres from the Dniester. Its Negru de Purcari, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Saperavi and Rară Neagră, won gold in Paris in 1878 and was served to Queen Victoria and Nicholas II; Pimen Cupcea recreated it after the Second World War. Revived since 2003, the château and its restored 1827 vaulted cellar anchor Purcari Wineries, now listed on the Bucharest stock exchange.

sites.name: Castel Mimi
sites.text: The winery Constantin Mimi, a Bessarabian governor trained in Montpellier, completed at Bulboaca around 1893 to 1901, considered the first true château of Bessarabia and built of reinforced concrete, then a novelty. Its cellar held about 300,000 litres. Restored between 2011 and 2016 as a winery, hotel and museum, it hosted the European Political Community summit in June 2023.

sites.name: Château Vartely
sites.text: A modern estate founded in 2004 on the outskirts of Orhei, with vineyards in Codru and the south, a hotel and one of Moldova's most visited wineries; known for Fetească Neagră, Rară Neagră and the Individo range.

sites.name: Asconi
sites.text: Family winery founded in 1994 at Puhoi, south-east of Chișinău, with a large tourist complex and a reputation for Fetească Neagră and sparkling wines.

sites.name: Et Cetera
sites.text: The Luchianov brothers' estate at Crocmaz, founded in 2002 in the Ștefan Vodă region near the Ukrainian border, a leader of Moldova's boutique wave with blends of Saperavi, Fetească Neagră and Bordeaux grapes.

sites.name: Gitana Winery (Tănătari)
sites.text: A small family winery in Tănătari, Căușeni district, known for low-yield reds such as its Lupi range of Rară Neagră and Fetească Neagră; the village sits between Codru and the Ștefan Vodă region.

sites.name: Château Cojușna
sites.text: A long-established winery at Cojușna, north-west of Chișinău, famous in Soviet times and now operating as Château Cojușna, with wine tunnels and tasting rooms in the Codru hills.

sites.name: Romănești estate
sites.text: The historic estate at Romănești, Strășeni, planted with Bordeaux varieties in the late nineteenth century, whose reds were reputedly reserved for the Kremlin in Soviet times; one of Moldova's first designations of origin protected in the EU.

sites.name: Ciumai
sites.text: Southern village in the Taraclia district, home of the historic Ciumai dessert wine and a large winery.

sites.name: Orheiul Vechi
sites.text: A dramatic limestone gorge of the Răut river with a cave monastery and medieval ruins, at the edge of the Codru wine region.

sites.name: Kvint distillery, Tiraspol
sites.text: Brandy distillery founded in 1897 in Tiraspol, in the breakaway Transnistria region; Kvint is the best-known producer of Moldovan divin-style brandy.

sites.name: Shabo wine culture centre
sites.text: The former Swiss colony of Chabag on the Dniester estuary, founded in 1822 by winegrowers from Vaud. Shabo, with about 1,200 hectares, is now Ukraine's largest wine company, with a museum of the colony.

sites.name: Massandra winery
sites.text: The imperial winery founded by Prince Lev Golitsyn in 1894 near Yalta, whose tunnel cellars hold about a million bottles, including dessert wines back to the eighteenth century. In occupied Crimea since 2014.

sites.name: Novy Svet sparkling wine cellars
sites.text: Prince Lev Golitsyn's estate near Sudak, where he dug cellars into the cliffs and made Russia's first great sparkling wine from the 1870s. In occupied Crimea since 2014.

sites.name: Inkerman winery
sites.text: Winery near Sevastopol that ages wine in limestone galleries left by quarrying. In occupied Crimea since 2014.

sites.name: Chersonesus
sites.text: The Greek city near Sevastopol (UNESCO), whose 'chora' of walled vineyard plots and wine presses is one of the best-preserved ancient agricultural landscapes anywhere.

sites.name: Koblevo
sites.text: A large winery on the Tylihul estuary between Odesa and Mykolaiv and one of Ukraine's best-known volume brands. Its vineyards sit on sandy chernozem by the estuary, where Black Sea air tempers the steppe heat.

sites.name: Chateau Chizay
sites.text: Winery near Berehove in Transcarpathia, on volcanic hills a few kilometres from the Hungarian border, part of a winegrowing area that shares soils and traditions with nearby Tokaj. It makes still and sparkling wines from Transcarpathian grapes.

sites.name: Prince Trubetskoi winery, Kozatske
sites.text: A historic estate on the Dnipro in Kherson oblast linked to Prince Trubetskoi, occupied in February 2022; its wine collection was looted and the chateau destroyed.

sites.name: Artwinery, Bakhmut
sites.text: Sparkling-wine plant founded in 1950 in former gypsum mines under Bakhmut; production moved to Odesa during the battle for the city.

sites.name: Abrau-Durso
sites.text: The imperial estate founded in 1870 beside Lake Abrau near Novorossiysk, where Prince Lev Golitsyn and French winemakers made Russia's first traditional-method sparkling wine for the tsars; the Soviet 'Sovetskoye Shampanskoye' style was modelled on it. Its tunnels run into the hills above the lake.

sites.name: Phanagoria
sites.text: The largest Greek city on the Taman peninsula, founded around 543 BC, with ancient wine presses and amphora workshops; the modern Fanagoria winery takes its name.

sites.name: Gorgippia
sites.text: The Greek city of Gorgippia, founded in the sixth century BC under modern Anapa, part of the Bosporan Kingdom; its open-air museum includes ancient wine-making installations and amphorae, evidence of wine on this coast for over two thousand years.

sites.name: Lefkadia
sites.text: Estate in the Lefkadia valley near Moldavanskoye in the Krymsk district of Kuban, planted from 2006; it holds its own protected designation of origin.

sites.name: Gai-Kodzor
sites.text: Village in the hills behind Anapa, a few kilometres from the Black Sea, where several of Kuban's new estates, including Gai-Kodzor winery, planted marl and limestone slopes from the 2000s.

sites.name: Tsimlyansk
sites.text: Town on the Don whose Cossack winemakers made the famous sparkling red Tsimlyanskoye from the native Tsimlyansky Cherny, praised by Pushkin. The Don valley around it is now the centre of a revival of Cossack grape varieties.

sites.name: Razdorskaya
sites.text: Cossack stanitsa on the Don, centre of the native-grape revival and home of an ethnographic museum.

sites.name: Shelek and Turgen vineyards
sites.text: The foothills of the Zailiysky Alatau east of Almaty around Shelek and Turgen, where Kazakhstan's new estates (including Arba Wine) grow vines that must be buried each winter.

sites.name: Khovrenko winery and museum, Samarkand
sites.text: Samarkand's historic winery at 58 Makhmud Kashgari street, founded in 1868 according to its own history by D. M. Filatov and later named after the Soviet oenologist M. A. Khovrenko. Its museum and tasting room present the sweet and fortified wines and brandies that made Samarkand known in the USSR.

sites.name: Afrasiyab
sites.text: The ancient city mound of Samarkand (Maracanda), capital of Sogdiana, whose merchants traded wine along the Silk Road.

sites.name: Ancient Panjakent
sites.text: Ruins of a Sogdian city on the Zeravshan, abandoned after the Arab conquest, with wine presses, storage jars and famous banquet murals.

sites.name: Old Nisa (Parthian fortress)
sites.text: The Parthian royal fortress near Ashgabat (UNESCO), whose archive of more than 2,000 inscribed potsherds records wine deliveries to the royal stores.

sites.name: Hajji Firuz Tepe
sites.text: A Neolithic mound in the Gadar valley south of Lake Urmia where six jars of about 5400 to 5000 BC, set in a kitchen floor, held tartaric acid and terebinth resin, the first chemical proof of ancient resinated wine (published 1996).

sites.name: Godin Tepe
sites.text: Late Uruk-period trading post in the central Zagros (about 3100 to 2900 BC) whose jars held wine and were stored lying on their sides.

sites.name: Tomb of Hafez, Shiraz
sites.text: The garden tomb of the fourteenth-century poet whose ghazals made wine the central metaphor of Persian poetry, in the city once famous for its wine.

sites.name: Persepolis
sites.text: Achaemenid ceremonial capital (UNESCO) whose administrative tablets record wine rations; reliefs show tribute bearers with vessels.

sites.name: Nimrud (Kalhu)
sites.text: The Assyrian capital Kalhu on the Tigris, whose 'wine lists' of the eighth century BC record wine rations issued to the royal household and palace staff. In Mesopotamia wine was a costly import from the northern hills.

sites.name: Nineveh
sites.text: Assyrian capital whose relief of Ashurbanipal's banquet shows the king drinking wine beneath a vine.
